infrastructure.air_sources.plain: How many facilities in each municipality the federal Clean Air Act regulates for what they emit into the air.
infrastructure.air_sources.plain_es: Cuántas instalaciones de cada municipio regula la Ley federal de Aire Limpio por lo que emiten al aire.
infrastructure.air_sources.definition: Active stationary sources of air pollution that the Clean Air Act regulates and EPA's ECHO lists: power plants, factories, quarries and asphalt plants, fuel terminals, hospitals and others with boilers, generators or processes that emit into the air, counted in the municipality that holds the facility's point.
infrastructure.air_sources.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active Clean Air Act facilities of Puerto Rico and downloads seven columns. Each of the 482 facilities counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 33 of them. 13 facilities that ECHO lists as temporarily closed are counted, because their permits are active. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 219 barrios hold one or more.
infrastructure.air_sources.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 482 such facilities in 65 municipalities; the most in San Juan 60, Guaynabo 31, Ponce 26. 438 of the 482 are not major sources.
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
Being regulated is not a violation: the count shows where permitted sources are, not where the air is dirty.
It is not a measure of air quality. Cars, trucks, ships, Saharan dust and other sources that are not facilities are not counted.
Most are minor sources, such as a business with an emergency generator; one large plant can emit more than many small ones.
A facility counts where it stands. Its emissions travel with the wind to other municipalities.
infrastructure.air_sources.source_detail: ECHO air_rest_services get_facilities (p_st=PR, p_act=Y) and get_download, columns SourceID, FacFIPSCode, FacLat, FacLong, AIRStatus, AIRClassification, AIRComplStatus

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: facilities regulated for air pollution

infrastructure.air_major.plain: How many of the facilities regulated for air pollution EPA classes as major sources.
infrastructure.air_major.plain_es: Cuántas de las instalaciones reguladas por contaminación del aire la EPA clasifica como fuentes mayores.
infrastructure.air_major.definition: Of the active facilities the Clean Air Act regulates, the ones EPA classes as major emissions sources (ECHO's classification): they emit, or could emit, more than the Act's thresholds, in most areas 100 tons a year of a regulated pollutant, or 10 tons a year of one hazardous air pollutant. A major source needs a Title V operating permit.
infrastructure.air_major.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active Clean Air Act facilities of Puerto Rico and downloads seven columns. Each of the 482 facilities counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 33 of them. 13 facilities that ECHO lists as temporarily closed are counted, because their permits are active. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 37 barrios hold one or more.
infrastructure.air_major.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 44 major sources in 27 municipalities; no municipality has more than 3.
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
Major is EPA's class for how much a facility emits or could emit, not a finding that it breaks its permit.
On 2026-11-11, ECHO showed 1 facility in Puerto Rico with a high priority violation. A number that small is not published for each municipality.
A facility counts where it stands. Its emissions travel with the wind to other municipalities.
Small counts: one facility more or less changes a municipality's value.
infrastructure.air_major.source_detail: ECHO air_rest_services get_facilities (p_st=PR, p_act=Y) and get_download, columns SourceID, FacFIPSCode, FacLat, FacLong, AIRStatus, AIRClassification, AIRComplStatus

infrastructure.bridges_poor.plain: How many highway bridges in each municipality are in poor condition, every year.
infrastructure.bridges_poor.plain_es: Cuántos puentes de carretera de cada municipio están en condición deficiente, cada año.
infrastructure.bridges_poor.definition: Bridges whose lowest rating of deck, superstructure, substructure or culvert is 4 or below (FHWA's definition of poor).
infrastructure.bridges_poor.method: infrastructure_series.py reads each year's Puerto Rico file and works out each bridge's condition by FHWA's rule (the lowest of the deck, superstructure, substructure and culvert ratings: 4 or below is poor, 7 or above good, the rest fair). In every year whose file gives FHWA's own condition column the two agree for every bridge; the build stops otherwise.
infrastructure.bridges_poor.how_to_read: 268 in 2016 and 344 in 2025 for Puerto Rico.
caveats: Poor does not mean unsafe: a bridge found unsafe is closed.
infrastructure.bridges_poor.source_detail: FHWA National Bridge Inventory, delimited file PR{yy}.txt for 2016-2025: COUNTY_CODE_003, DECK_COND_058, SUPERSTRUCTURE_COND_059, SUBSTRUCTURE_COND_060, CULVERT_COND_062, BRIDGE_CONDITION

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: bridges in poor condition

infrastructure.bridges_poor_pct.plain: Out of every 100 highway bridges in each municipality, how many are in poor condition, every year.
infrastructure.bridges_poor_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 puentes de carretera de cada municipio, cuántos están en condición deficiente, cada año.
infrastructure.bridges_poor_pct.definition: Bridges in poor condition (FHWA's definition) divided by all of the municipality's bridges, by count, times 100.
infrastructure.bridges_poor_pct.method: infrastructure_series.py reads each year's Puerto Rico file and works out each bridge's condition by FHWA's rule (the lowest of the deck, superstructure, substructure and culvert ratings: 4 or below is poor, 7 or above good, the rest fair). In every year whose file gives FHWA's own condition column the two agree for every bridge; the build stops otherwise.
infrastructure.bridges_poor_pct.how_to_read: 11.61% in 2016 and 14.13% in 2025 for Puerto Rico.
caveats: A municipality with few bridges can swing widely.
By count, not by deck area.
infrastructure.bridges_poor_pct.source_detail: FHWA National Bridge Inventory, delimited file PR{yy}.txt for 2016-2025: COUNTY_CODE_003, DECK_COND_058, SUPERSTRUCTURE_COND_059, SUBSTRUCTURE_COND_060, CULVERT_COND_062, BRIDGE_CONDITION

infrastructure.bridges.plain_es: Cuántos puentes de carretera hay en cada municipio, cada año.
infrastructure.bridges.definition: Bridges of the public road network in the National Bridge Inventory (spans longer than 20 feet), in the municipality the inventory gives.
infrastructure.bridges.method: infrastructure_series.py reads each year's Puerto Rico file and works out each bridge's condition by FHWA's rule (the lowest of the deck, superstructure, substructure and culvert ratings: 4 or below is poor, 7 or above good, the rest fair). In every year whose file gives FHWA's own condition column the two agree for every bridge; the build stops otherwise.
infrastructure.bridges.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 2,308 bridges in 2016 and 2,434 in 2025.
caveats: New or newly inventoried bridges raise the count.

layers.broadband_hex.plain: A map layer of small hexagons that shows where home internet of 100/20 Mbps or more is missing, from what providers report to the FCC. Darker hexagons have a larger share of homes and businesses that cannot get it.
layers.broadband_hex.plain_es: Una capa del mapa de hexágonos pequeños que muestra dónde falta internet en casa de 100/20 Mbps o más, según lo que los proveedores informan a la FCC. Los hexágonos más oscuros tienen una mayor proporción de hogares y negocios que no pueden tenerlo.
layers.broadband_hex.definition: broadband_hex.geojson: one hexagon for each H3 cell of resolution 8 that holds 10 or more broadband serviceable locations in the FCC's newest June release (9,971 hexagons with 1,162,059 locations as of 2026-06-30). Each has h (the H3 cell), n (locations), below_pct (the share underserved or unserved: no 100/20 Mbps over a reliable technology with low latency), unserved_pct (below 25/3), fiber_pct (fiber to the premises from any provider) and mun (the municipio that holds most of its locations). 3,800 cells with fewer than 10 locations (15,256 locations) are counted in the file's notes and not drawn.
layers.broadband_hex.method: broadband.py reads the FCC's Puerto Rico state location files of the newest June release with FPR's FCC account (GitHub Actions), gives each location its best tier (NTIA BEAD: served 100/20 Mbps or more, underserved 25/3 to 100/20, unserved below, over copper, cable, fiber or licensed fixed wireless with low latency) and its fiber flag, and counts the locations in the H3 cell the FCC gives each one (h3_res8_id). Outlines come from the h3 library (cell_to_boundary), to 4 decimals. Cells with fewer than 10 locations are not drawn (HANDOFF decision 101 (b)). The 2D map (js/facilities.js) and the 3D view (js/facilities3d.js) draw it from the shared list core/facilities.js, in the classes of the Broadband gaps page (below 1, 1-5, 5-15, 15-35, 35% and over), so any map that reads that list draws it too.
layers.broadband_hex.how_to_read: As of 2026-06-30, 9,971 hexagons hold 1,162,059 of Puerto Rico's 1,177,315 locations. Read a dark hexagon as a place where many homes and businesses lack 100/20 Mbps, and look at its number of locations in the pop-up: a hexagon of 12 locations is a handful of homes.
caveats: Availability is what providers report they can install within ten business days, not what anyone subscribes to or the speed they get.
Hexagons with fewer than 10 locations, mostly in the mountains and on the edges, are not drawn, so the gaps there are under-shown on the map; the Broadband gaps page counts them by barrio.
A hexagon is a fixed grid cell, not a neighbourhood: it can cut across a barrio or a municipio line.
layers.broadband_hex.source_detail: FCC Broadband Data Collection, fixed broadband availability, Puerto Rico state location files as of 2026-06-30 (https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/data-download). H3: Uber Technologies, H3 hexagonal grid (https://h3geo.org/).

view.label: Map, Layers tab: Infrastructure and mobility, Communications

methods.broadband.plain: Where homes and businesses can get fast internet at home, from what internet providers report to the FCC twice a year: how many places are served at 100/20 Mbps or more, underserved or unserved, and where fiber is available, for every barrio and municipio since 2023.
methods.broadband.plain_es: Dónde los hogares y negocios pueden tener internet rápido en casa, según lo que los proveedores informan a la FCC dos veces al año: cuántos lugares tienen servicio de 100/20 Mbps o más, servicio insuficiente o ninguno, y dónde hay fibra, para cada barrio y municipio desde 2023.
methods.broadband.definition: Each broadband serviceable location in the FCC's Puerto Rico files gets one tier from the best low-latency service it can get over a reliable technology: served (100/20 Mbps or more), underserved (25/3 or more, below 100/20) or unserved (below 25/3, or none), as NTIA's BEAD program defines them; fiber is any provider reporting fiber to the premises. Counts are summed by 2020 census block, then by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico.
methods.broadband.method: broadband.py, in GitHub Actions with FPR's FCC account (secrets FCC_BDC_USERNAME and FCC_BDC_HASH), lists the BDC releases, keeps the June 30 release of each year from 2023, and downloads Puerto Rico's state location files for every fixed technology (copper, cable, fiber, satellite, licensed, licensed-by-rule and unlicensed fixed wireless). Each row is a location, a provider and a technology with its maximum advertised speeds and a low-latency flag. The build gives each location its best tier, sums the locations by census block (block_geoid), places each block in its barrio by the Census Bureau's internal point, and publishes only counts and shares by area. Checks at every build: 900,000 to 1,500,000 locations, every municipio with locations, every block known. In this build the June 2025 count of served locations (1,108,862) is within 0.04% of the figure Esri's Living Atlas copy of the same FCC data gives (1,109,321).
methods.broadband.how_to_read: As of June 30, 2026, Puerto Rico had 1,177,315 broadband serviceable locations: 95.4% served at 100/20 Mbps or more, 1.2% underserved and 3.4% unserved; fiber was available at 70.6% of them, up from 46.3% in June 2023.
caveats: Availability is what providers report they can install within ten business days; it is not what households subscribe to (see the survey's households with an internet subscription) or the speed they get.
Providers' reports can be challenged and corrected; the FCC publishes each release again as challenges are settled, so a figure can move a little between versions of the same release.
The FCC's list of locations (the Fabric) changes between releases, so part of a change from one year to the next comes from the list, not from the networks.
A barrio with few locations moves a lot from one release to the next: read several years together.
methods.broadband.source_detail: FCC Broadband Data Collection, fixed broadband availability, Puerto Rico state location files (category State, subcategory Location Coverage), June releases 2023-2026; newest as of 2026-06-30, published by the FCC on 2026-10-24 (https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/data-download). Tiers: NTIA, BEAD Notice of Funding Opportunity (2022). Census blocks and barrio outlines: TIGER/Line 2020.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: broadband

infrastructure.water_nonprasa.plain: How many community water systems outside PRASA, most of them run by the community itself, serve each municipality.
infrastructure.water_nonprasa.plain_es: Cuántos sistemas comunitarios de agua fuera de la AAA (non-PRASA), la mayoría administrados por la propia comunidad, sirven a cada municipio.
infrastructure.water_nonprasa.definition: Active community water systems that the Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS) records as privately owned, through EPA ECHO. EPA Region 2 defines the non-PRASA systems as the privately owned ones; most are run by community associations in the mountains, a few serve private developments or institutions. A system serving several municipalities counts in each.
infrastructure.water_nonprasa.method: infrastructure_series.py reads the owner type of each active community water system from the same ECHO download as water_systems and counts the privately owned ones (owner type P) in every municipality their FIPS codes name. Puerto Rico's value counts each system once. No name is kept.
infrastructure.water_nonprasa.how_to_read: 207 systems in Puerto Rico report serving 100,743 people. The most are in San Lorenzo 14, Orocovis 13, Caguas 13 and Utuado 12. 31 municipalities have none. 201 of the 207 carry ECHO's health-based violation flag (infrastructure_series.json notes).
caveats: SDWIS records some community-run systems as local government, the owner type of PRASA's systems, so this count can miss a few: EPA Region 2 counted 241 non-PRASA community systems serving about 93,500 people in 2025.

No federal source gives where these systems are below the municipality, and their names often carry a person's or a family's name, so the observatory publishes counts only (wanted.json: non-prasa-locations).
A violation flag is a compliance record, not proof that the water is unsafe today.
infrastructure.water_nonprasa.source_detail: ECHO sdw_rest_services get_download, column OwnerTypeCode = P

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: community water systems outside PRASA

infrastructure.water_systems.plain: How many community water systems serve each municipality: PRASA's systems and the community-run ones.
infrastructure.water_systems.plain_es: Cuántos sistemas comunitarios de agua sirven a cada municipio: los de la AAA y los comunitarios.
infrastructure.water_systems.definition: Active community water systems that list the municipality among those they serve (EPA ECHO). A system serving several municipalities counts in each.
infrastructure.water_systems.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active community water systems of Puerto Rico and downloads seven columns. Each system counts in every municipality its FIPS codes name; 28 systems serve two to four municipalities and 5 small ones give no municipality (Puerto Rico's code only): they count in the island value only. Puerto Rico's value counts each system once, so the municipal values add up to more. The system's name is never kept.
infrastructure.water_systems.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 404 active community water systems, which together serve about 3,295,853 people. The most are in Ponce 21, Caguas 20, Orocovis 18: municipalities with many small community-run systems.
caveats: The municipal values add up to more than Puerto Rico's, which counts each system once.
Population served is not given per municipality: a large system's people cannot be split honestly among the municipalities it serves.
infrastructure.water_systems.source_detail: ECHO sdw_rest_services get_systems (p_st=PR, p_act=Y, p_systyp=CWS) and get_download, columns PWSId, PWSTypeCode, PopulationServedCount, OwnerTypeCode, SeriousViolator, HealthFlag, FIPSCodes

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: community water systems serving the municipality

infrastructure.water_nonprasa_pop.plain: How many people get their water from a community system outside PRASA, as the systems report it, in each municipality.
infrastructure.water_nonprasa_pop.plain_es: Cuántas personas reciben el agua de un sistema comunitario fuera de la AAA, según lo informan los sistemas, en cada municipio.
infrastructure.water_nonprasa_pop.definition: The population that the non-PRASA systems (privately owned in SDWIS) report serving, added up for the systems that serve only this municipality. Shaded per 1,000 residents, it approximates the share of residents on a non-PRASA system.
infrastructure.water_nonprasa_pop.method: infrastructure_series.py adds the PopulationServedCount of each non-PRASA system to its municipality when the system serves one municipality only. The 5 systems that serve two municipalities (1,087 people) and one that names no municipality (165 people) are left out of every municipality's value and counted in Puerto Rico's.
infrastructure.water_nonprasa_pop.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 100,743 people. Lares 17,278, Yabucoa 6,573, Naranjito 5,840, Caguas 4,958.
caveats: The population served is each system's own estimate to the regulator, not a census count.
The municipal values add up to less than Puerto Rico's: systems that serve two municipalities are left out of both, because their population cannot be split.
Systems recorded as local government are not included (see Community water systems outside PRASA).
infrastructure.water_nonprasa_pop.source_detail: ECHO sdw_rest_services get_download, columns PopulationServedCount, OwnerTypeCode = P, FIPSCodes

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: residents served by community water systems outside PRASA

infrastructure.water_priority.plain: How many of the water systems serving each municipality EPA treats as a priority for enforcement.
infrastructure.water_priority.plain_es: Cuántos de los sistemas de agua que sirven a cada municipio la EPA trata como prioridad de cumplimiento.
infrastructure.water_priority.definition: Systems that EPA designates as an enforcement priority: unresolved serious, multiple or continuing violations (ECHO's SeriousViolator).
infrastructure.water_priority.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active community water systems of Puerto Rico and downloads seven columns. Each system counts in every municipality its FIPS codes name; 28 systems serve two to four municipalities and 5 small ones give no municipality (Puerto Rico's code only): they count in the island value only. Puerto Rico's value counts each system once, so the municipal values add up to more. The system's name is never kept.
infrastructure.water_priority.how_to_read: 125 systems in Puerto Rico; the most in Utuado 12, Adjuntas 8, Ponce 8.
caveats: Priority for formal enforcement under EPA's response policy; many systems with violations are not designated.
infrastructure.water_priority.source_detail: ECHO sdw_rest_services get_systems (p_st=PR, p_act=Y, p_systyp=CWS) and get_download, columns PWSId, PWSTypeCode, PopulationServedCount, OwnerTypeCode, SeriousViolator, HealthFlag, FIPSCodes

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: water systems that are an enforcement priority

infrastructure.water_health_vio.plain: How many of the water systems serving each municipality EPA flags with a health-based violation.
infrastructure.water_health_vio.plain_es: Cuántos de los sistemas de agua que sirven a cada municipio tienen una violación basada en la salud según la EPA.
infrastructure.water_health_vio.definition: Systems that ECHO flags with a health-based violation: a breach of a maximum contaminant level, a maximum residual disinfectant level or a treatment technique rule (ECHO's HealthFlag).
infrastructure.water_health_vio.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active community water systems of Puerto Rico and downloads seven columns. Each system counts in every municipality its FIPS codes name; 28 systems serve two to four municipalities and 5 small ones give no municipality (Puerto Rico's code only): they count in the island value only. Puerto Rico's value counts each system once, so the municipal values add up to more. The system's name is never kept.
infrastructure.water_health_vio.how_to_read: 239 of Puerto Rico's 404 systems carry the flag; the most in Caguas 17, San Lorenzo 14, Adjuntas 13.
caveats: A compliance record, not proof that the water is unsafe today.
ECHO's flag covers recent years of violations; read a system's own report on ECHO for its dates.
infrastructure.water_health_vio.source_detail: ECHO sdw_rest_services get_systems (p_st=PR, p_act=Y, p_systyp=CWS) and get_download, columns PWSId, PWSTypeCode, PopulationServedCount, OwnerTypeCode, SeriousViolator, HealthFlag, FIPSCodes

layers.fire_stations.plain: Fire and emergency medical service stations on the map, with their name, type and municipio.
layers.fire_stations.plain_es: Las estaciones de bomberos y de emergencias médicas en el mapa, con su nombre, tipo y municipio.
layers.fire_stations.definition: fire_stations.geojson: one point per station of the USGS National Structures Dataset, with name, type, municipio and geoid. 94 stations on 2026-10-17.
layers.fire_stations.method: facilities.py reads USGS layer 51 for Puerto Rico and places each station in the municipio that holds its point. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js, which holds its file, colour, pop-up and note.
layers.fire_stations.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Community services, Safety and emergencies: Fire and EMS stations). Both views draw the same points, with the same note on what is counted but not drawn and the same pop-up. Click a point for the station's name, type, municipio and source.
caveats: A station can be missing, moved or closed since USGS last edited it.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Fire and EMS stations
3D view, Layers tab: Fire and EMS stations

facilities.fire_stations.plain: How many fire and emergency medical service stations each municipio has, as the US Geological Survey maps them.
facilities.fire_stations.plain_es: Cuántas estaciones de bomberos y de emergencias médicas tiene cada municipio, según el Servicio Geológico de EE. UU.
facilities.fire_stations.definition: Fire stations and emergency medical service (EMS) stations in the USGS National Structures Dataset (feature code 74026), in the municipio that holds each point.
facilities.fire_stations.method: facilities.py queries layer 51 of USGS's structures map service for state = 'PR' and places each station by point in polygon against the municipio outlines (a point on the coast within 2 km of a municipio counts there).
facilities.fire_stations.how_to_read: USGS maps 94 fire and EMS stations in Puerto Rico: San Juan 7, Ponce 4. One municipio has none in the dataset.
caveats: USGS collects structures for emergency planning; a station can be missing or closed. OpenStreetMap had 77 fire stations on 2026-10-17, 74 of them within 500 m of a USGS station.
Fire and EMS stations are one category in the source and cannot be told apart.
facilities.fire_stations.source_detail: USGS TNM structures MapServer layer 51 (Fire Stations/EMS Stations), fields permanent_identifier, name, fcode, state, loaddate

layers.police_stations.plain: Police stations as volunteers mapped them in OpenStreetMap, with their name, type and municipio.
layers.police_stations.plain_es: Los cuarteles de la policía tal como los trazaron los voluntarios de OpenStreetMap, con su nombre, tipo y municipio.
layers.police_stations.definition: police_stations.geojson: one point per OpenStreetMap police feature (amenity=police; a building outline is drawn at its centre), with name (15 have none), type (municipal police, state police, or agency not stated, read from the name and operator tags), municipio, geoid and osm (the OpenStreetMap element, such as n123 for a node or w456 for a way). 141 stations on 2026-10-17.
layers.police_stations.method: facilities.py asks the Overpass API for amenity=police in Puerto Rico, places each feature by point in polygon and counts a station mapped twice (same name, within 30 m) once. The type is 'Municipal police' when the name or operator says municipal, 'State police' when it names the Policía de Puerto Rico or the state police, else 'agency not stated'. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js, which holds its file, colour, pop-up and note.
layers.police_stations.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Community services, Safety and emergencies: Police stations). Both views draw the same points, with the same note on what is counted but not drawn and the same pop-up. Click a point for the station's name, type, municipio and source. Anyone can add a missing station at openstreetmap.org.
caveats: Volunteers map these; stations are likely missing, and a few features are other police facilities.
ODbL: credit OpenStreetMap contributors; a database built on this file must be shared alike.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Police stations
3D view, Layers tab: Police stations

facilities.police_stations.plain: How many police stations volunteers have mapped in each municipio in OpenStreetMap.
facilities.police_stations.plain_es: Cuántos cuarteles de la policía han trazado los voluntarios de OpenStreetMap en cada municipio.
facilities.police_stations.definition: Features tagged amenity=police in OpenStreetMap (state and municipal police stations and a few other police facilities), in the municipio that holds each point. A station mapped twice (a point and its building with the same name, within 30 m) counts once.
facilities.police_stations.method: facilities.py asks the Overpass API for every amenity=police node, way and relation in Puerto Rico's bounding box (a building's centre stands for it) and places each by point in polygon. 144 features gave 141 stations on 2026-10-17.
facilities.police_stations.how_to_read: OpenStreetMap has 141 police stations in Puerto Rico: San Juan 24, Ponce 8, Guaynabo 6. Fifteen municipios have none mapped, which more likely means a gap in the map than no station.
caveats: Volunteers map these; a missing station is likely. USGS had only 8 police stations for Puerto Rico, so OpenStreetMap is the more complete source.
A few features are other police facilities (a highway patrol, a maritime unit, a watchtower), as they are tagged.
OpenStreetMap data are under the ODbL: credit OpenStreetMap contributors.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: police stations

infrastructure.epa_inspected.plain: How many regulated facilities in each municipality had an environmental inspection in the last five years.
infrastructure.epa_inspected.plain_es: Cuántas instalaciones reguladas de cada municipio tuvieron una inspección ambiental en los últimos cinco años.
infrastructure.epa_inspected.definition: Of the active facilities that EPA regulates under the air, water, hazardous waste or drinking water laws, the ones that EPA or the Puerto Rico government inspected at least once in the last five years, counted in the municipality that holds the facility's point.
infrastructure.epa_inspected.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active facilities of Puerto Rico in every program (3,925 on 2026-11-12) and downloads six columns. A facility counts once, however many inspections or actions it had, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point. 1 facility whose point is off the island is placed by ECHO's county code, and 2 with neither are left out. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept.
infrastructure.epa_inspected.how_to_read: 594 of Puerto Rico's 3,925 regulated facilities were inspected in the last five years (1,074 inspections in all); the most in San Juan 35, Caguas 24, Guaynabo 21.

A facility counts once, however many actions it received.

infrastructure.hazwaste_handlers.plain: How many businesses and institutions in each municipality generate, transport, treat or store hazardous waste under federal rules.

infrastructure.hazwaste_handlers.definition: Active handlers of hazardous waste that EPA's ECHO lists under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA): the businesses and institutions that generate hazardous waste (factories, laboratories, hospitals, auto shops, dry cleaners and others), and those that transport, treat or store it, counted in the municipality that holds the handler's point.
infrastructure.hazwaste_handlers.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active hazardous waste handlers of Puerto Rico and downloads six columns. Each of the 1,740 handlers counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 113 of them. A handler that is in several classes (a large quantity generator that is also a transporter) counts once. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The handler's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 389 barrios hold one or more.
infrastructure.hazwaste_handlers.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 1,740 handlers in 75 municipalities; the most in San Juan 287, Bayamón 117, Carolina 116. 1,203 of them generate very small quantities (less than 100 kilograms a month).
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
Being a handler is not a violation: the count shows where hazardous waste is generated or managed under the rules, not where it has been spilled or dumped.
Most handlers generate very small amounts, such as an auto shop or a pharmacy; the count follows where businesses are.
The count does not give the amount or the kind of waste.
Household hazardous waste and illegal dumping are not in ECHO.

economy.crime_murders.plain: How many murders the Police recorded in a municipality in a year.
economy.crime_murders.definition: The murder column (asesinatos) of the Police's December report: murders and non-negligent homicides recorded in the municipality from 1 January to 31 December.
economy.crime_murders.method: economy_series.py, function police_values: the murder column of the municipality table (see economy.crime_type1 for how the table is read and checked).
economy.crime_murders.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 463 murders in 2025 and 679 in 2017 (2026-10 snapshot). San Juan had 82 in 2025, about 18% of the island. The island figures match the homicides that the FBI's Crime Data Explorer shows for Puerto Rico within 5 in every year from 2018 to 2024 (for example 606 in 2019 and 529 in 2020 in both).
caveats: Counts are small in most municipalities: 9 had no murder in 2025. One or two cases change a small municipality's rate a lot, so look at several years before comparing places.
The year is when the murder happened, as recorded in the December report. A death that the Police reclassify later is not updated here.
economy.crime_murders.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the TOTAL row of each report)
economy.crime_murders.source_detail: Policía de Puerto Rico, Type I crimes by municipality (December report)

economy.crime_property.plain: How many burglaries, thefts and stolen vehicles people reported to the Police in a municipality in a year.
economy.crime_property.definition: The sum of three of the eight Type I crimes in the Police's December report: burglary (escalamiento), larceny (apropiación ilegal) and vehicle theft (vehículo hurtado), recorded in the municipality from 1 January to 31 December.
economy.crime_property.method: economy_series.py, function police_values: the sum of the burglary, larceny and vehicle theft columns of the municipality table (see economy.crime_type1 for how the table is read and checked).
economy.crime_property.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 14,031 property Type I crimes reported in 2025 (2026-10 snapshot), 10,001 of them larcenies. Per 1,000 residents in 2025 the highest were San Juan (10.8) and Culebra (10.4), places with many visitors, and the lowest Sabana Grande (0.7).
caveats: Most of the fall in Type I crimes after 2019 is here: 22,152 property crimes in 2019, 13,052 in 2020. The reports do not say why (see economy.crime_type1).
Thefts are often not reported when nothing is insured or recovered, so reporting rates differ a lot between places and years.
A rate per resident leaves out visitors and shoppers, who are often the victims of thefts in tourist and shopping areas.
economy.crime_property.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the TOTAL row of each report)
economy.crime_property.source_detail: Policía de Puerto Rico, Type I crimes by municipality (December report)

economy.crime_type1.plain: How many of the eight most serious crimes people reported to the Police in a municipality in a year. It counts complaints, not every crime that happened.
economy.crime_type1.definition: Complaints (querellas) of the eight Type I crimes that the Policía de Puerto Rico recorded in the municipality from 1 January to 31 December: murder, rape, human trafficking, robbery, aggravated assault, burglary (escalamiento), larceny (apropiación ilegal) and vehicle theft. Type I follows the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) model of the FBI as the Police describe it. Taken from the municipality table of the Police's December report, which the Instituto de Estadísticas de Puerto Rico publishes.
economy.crime_type1.method: economy_series.py, functions police_table, police and police_values. For each year the build downloads the December report: an Excel file (.xls) for 2017 to 2022, read from the sheet MUNICIPIO or MUNICIPIOS with xlrd, and a ZIP of PDFs from 2023, of which it reads the municipality table with pdftotext. Each row is a municipality name and nine counts. The build finds the total among the nine counts as the one that equals the sum of the other eight (it comes first in 2017 to 2023 and last from 2024). Names are matched to the 78 municipalities ignoring accents and capitals; the 2024 table writes Sabana Grande as SABANA. The build stops if any year does not match all 78 municipalities, if the 78 rows do not add up to the report's TOTAL row in every column, or if a municipality's total is not the sum of its eight crimes. The counts are kept in cache/economy/police_type1.json and written to economy_series.json; `python economy_series.py --police` updates only these series.
economy.crime_type1.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 20,463 Type I crimes reported in 2025 (2026-10 snapshot); San Juan had 4,760 of them. Large municipalities have more crimes because they have more people, so compare places per 1,000 residents (the Analysis tab's 'per resident' option). In 2025, per 1,000 residents, the highest were San Juan (14.4), Culebra (11.5) and Loíza (11.4) and the lowest Sabana Grande (1.7). About two of every three Type I crimes are property crimes, so this total mostly follows economy.crime_property; read economy.crime_violent for violence.
caveats: These are crimes reported to and recorded by the Police. Crimes nobody reports are missing, and how often people report differs by crime and by place, so a low count is not proof of a safe place.

The island total fell from 28,517 in 2019 to 18,206 in 2020 and has stayed near 20,000 since. Property crimes account for most of the drop. The reports do not explain it: the 2020 pandemic is one likely reason, but a change in how crimes are recorded cannot be ruled out. Compare years before and after 2020 with care.

A rate per resident counts only the people who live in the municipality. Places with many visitors or commuters, such as San Juan, Culebra and other tourist and shopping areas, look worse per resident than per person present.
Small municipalities have small counts, so their rates can swing widely from one year to the next.
Each year comes from the December report as first published. The Police can revise figures later; the observatory does not.

These figures are not the Police's public crime map (incidenciacriminal.policia.pr.gov), which counts all offences of the National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS) for the current year only. The two do not match and should not be compared.
The source states no license. Check with the Instituto de Estadísticas or the Police before reusing the figures.

economy.crime_type1.source_detail: Policía de Puerto Rico, División de Estadísticas de la Criminalidad, Delitos Tipo I, municipality table of the December reports for 2017 to 2025, downloaded 2026-10-06 from estadisticas.pr (2017 to 2024) and estadisticas.pr.gov (2025).

economy.crime_violent.plain: How many murders, rapes, cases of human trafficking, robberies and aggravated assaults people reported to the Police in a municipality in a year.
economy.crime_violent.definition: The sum of five of the eight Type I crimes in the Police's December report: murder, rape, human trafficking, robbery and aggravated assault, recorded in the municipality from 1 January to 31 December. Aggravated assault is most of it.
economy.crime_violent.method: economy_series.py, function police_values: the sum of the murder, rape, human trafficking, robbery and aggravated assault columns of the municipality table (see economy.crime_type1 for how the table is read and checked).
economy.crime_violent.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 6,432 violent Type I crimes reported in 2025 (2026-10 snapshot), 4,472 of them aggravated assaults. Per 1,000 residents in 2025 the highest were Loíza (4.2) and Guayama (4.2) and the lowest Hormigueros (0.5). For 2018 the island figure (6,407) is within 0.2% of the violent crime count that the FBI's Crime Data Explorer shows for Puerto Rico (6,417).
caveats: Reported crimes only. Rape and other sexual crimes in particular are known to be under-reported everywhere.
Do not use the FBI's Crime Data Explorer to extend this series: from 2021 its 'violent crime' figure for Puerto Rico equals the number of homicides, so it stops counting the other violent crimes.
A rate per resident leaves out visitors and commuters, and small municipalities can swing widely from year to year (see economy.crime_type1).

infrastructure.tri_air_lb.plain: How many pounds of listed toxic chemicals the reporting facilities of each municipality released to the air in a year.
infrastructure.tri_air_lb.plain_es: Cuántas libras de sustancias químicas tóxicas listadas liberaron al aire en un año las instalaciones de cada municipio que informan.
infrastructure.tri_air_lb.definition: Of the pounds the TRI facilities released in 2024, the ones released on site to the air: from stacks and vents (stack air) and as leaks and evaporation (fugitive air). Summed for the municipality that holds each facility's point.
infrastructure.tri_air_lb.method: infrastructure_series.py downloads EPA's TRI Basic Data File for Puerto Rico (reporting year 2024: 104 facilities), which has one row for each facility and chemical. It adds each facility's pounds (dioxins, reported in grams, are converted) and sums them for the municipality whose boundary holds the facility's point. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the facilities. Values are whole pounds. The facility's name is never read, and its point is not published.
infrastructure.tri_air_lb.how_to_read: In 2024 the facilities reported 1,264,140 pounds released to the air, of 2,686,420 pounds in all; the most in Peñuelas 384,761, Guayama 316,292, Salinas 119,868.
caveats: Pounds of different chemicals are added together, so the figure shows amount, not toxicity or risk.
It is not a measure of air quality: the wind carries a release away from the municipality where the facility stands.
Only larger facilities in certain industries report, and only for the chemicals on EPA's list.
18 of the 43 municipalities with a reporting facility have only one: there the figure is that facility's own public report.
infrastructure.tri_air_lb.source_detail: TRI Basic Data File, Puerto Rico: columns 2 (TRIFD), 12-13 (point), 50 (unit), 51-52 (fugitive and stack air), 107 (total releases)

infrastructure.tri_release_lb.plain_es: Cuántas libras de sustancias químicas tóxicas listadas liberaron en un año las instalaciones de cada municipio que informan.
infrastructure.tri_release_lb.definition: The pounds of listed toxic chemicals that the facilities reporting to EPA's Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) released in 2024: on site, to the air, to water and to land, and off site, sent elsewhere for disposal. Summed for the municipality that holds each facility's point.
infrastructure.tri_release_lb.method: infrastructure_series.py downloads EPA's TRI Basic Data File for Puerto Rico (reporting year 2024: 104 facilities), which has one row for each facility and chemical. It adds each facility's pounds (dioxins, reported in grams, are converted) and sums them for the municipality whose boundary holds the facility's point. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the facilities. Values are whole pounds. The facility's name is never read, and its point is not published.
infrastructure.tri_release_lb.how_to_read: In 2024, 104 facilities in 43 municipalities reported 2,686,420 pounds; the most in Guayama 919,665, Ponce 575,010, Peñuelas 384,782. One facility reported 32.6% of the total.
caveats: Pounds of different chemicals are added together: a pound of one chemical can be far more harmful than a pound of another, so the figure shows amount, not toxicity or risk.
A release is reported and usually allowed by a permit; it is not by itself a violation.
Only larger facilities in certain industries report, and only for the chemicals on EPA's list. Smaller sources and vehicles are not counted.
18 of the 43 municipalities with a reporting facility have only one: there the figure is that facility's own public report.
A facility counts where it stands. What it releases to the air or to water travels to other municipalities.
The amounts are the facilities' own estimates.

economy.internet_subscription_pct.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many pay for any kind of internet service, including a cellular data plan. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 81.4% in 2020-2024, up from 53.8% in 2013-2017.
economy.internet_subscription_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos pagan por algún tipo de servicio de internet, incluido un plan de datos celulares. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 81.4% en 2020-2024, más que el 53.8% de 2013-2017.
economy.internet_subscription_pct.definition: Households with an internet subscription of any type divided by all households, times 100 (American Community Survey, ACS, table B28002: cell 2, 'With an Internet subscription', over cell 1, all households). Cell 2 includes dial-up, broadband of any type (cable, fiber optic, DSL, satellite) and a cellular data plan, alone or with others. The series starts with the 2013-2017 window, which the Analysis tab shows under the label 2017.
economy.internet_subscription_pct.method: The observatory reads table B28002 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 2 by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one. The series starts with the 2013-2017 window (labeled 2017). The Census Bureau's Puerto Rico summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2016 do not contain table B28002, so no earlier value exists.
economy.internet_subscription_pct.how_to_read: A value of 81 means that 81 of every 100 households had an internet subscription. A household that has only a cellular data plan counts as subscribed, so the share does not tell you how many homes have fixed broadband. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the change from 53.8% to 81.4% between 2013-2017 and 2020-2024 is large next to the margins. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B28002 (Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household), cell 2 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The series starts with the 2013-2017 window, shown under the label 2017. The Census Bureau's Puerto Rico summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2016 do not contain table B28002, so no earlier value exists. The data do not show whether households were asked the internet questions in every year of the first window, so check the Census Bureau's documentation before you treat it as a full five-year window.
If you choose a year before 2017 on the Analysis tab, the map shows the 2013-2017 value and labels it 'first data 2017'. There is no earlier value.

Windows that include 2017 (2013-2017 to 2017-2021) or 2020 (2016-2020 to 2020-2024) carry survey disruption: see 'Census tables behind the income, worker, commuting and internet figures' (economy.acs_work_income_tables). The change between windows mixes real change with these effects.

This share and the share with no internet access do not add to 100. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the rest are households with internet access but no subscription (cell 12): 1.7% in Puerto Rico for 2020-2024 and 3.2% for 2013-2017.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.8 to ±9.3 points across the 78 municipalities, and none is larger than 30% of the estimate. In the same snapshot, Las Marías has the lowest value for 2020-2024, 38.3% (± 5.8 points).

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 81.5% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 81.4%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Cabo Rojo goes from 39.06% (2016-2020) to 52.64% (2017-2021). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 16% of barrios and less than 1% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.

economy.no_internet_pct.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many report no internet access of any kind: no paid subscription and no free access. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 16.9% in 2020-2024, down from 43.0% in 2013-2017.
economy.no_internet_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos informan que no tienen acceso a internet de ningún tipo: ni suscripción pagada ni acceso gratis. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 16.9% en 2020-2024, menos que el 43.0% de 2013-2017.
economy.no_internet_pct.definition: Households with no internet access divided by all households, times 100 (American Community Survey, ACS, table B28002: cell 13, 'No Internet access', over cell 1, all households). Households that use the internet without paying for a subscription are in cell 12 and are not counted here. The series starts with the 2013-2017 window, which the Analysis tab shows under the label 2017.
economy.no_internet_pct.method: The observatory reads table B28002 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 13 by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one. The series starts with the 2013-2017 window (labeled 2017). The Census Bureau's Puerto Rico summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2016 do not contain table B28002, so no earlier value exists.
economy.no_internet_pct.how_to_read: A value of 17 means that 17 of every 100 households had no internet access. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it fell island-wide from 43.0% in 2013-2017 to 16.9% in 2020-2024. It is not the opposite of the subscription share: the two do not add to 100. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B28002 (Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household), cell 13 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The series starts with the 2013-2017 window, shown under the label 2017. The Census Bureau's Puerto Rico summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2016 do not contain table B28002, so no earlier value exists. The data do not show whether households were asked the internet questions in every year of the first window, so check the Census Bureau's documentation before you treat it as a full five-year window.
If you choose a year before 2017 on the Analysis tab, the map shows the 2013-2017 value and labels it 'first data 2017'. There is no earlier value.

Windows that include 2017 (2013-2017 to 2017-2021) or 2020 (2016-2020 to 2020-2024) carry survey disruption: see 'Census tables behind the income, worker, commuting and internet figures' (economy.acs_work_income_tables). The change between windows mixes real change with these effects.

This share and the share with a subscription do not add to 100. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the rest are households with internet access but no subscription (cell 12): 1.7% in Puerto Rico for 2020-2024 and 3.2% for 2013-2017.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.8 to ±8.5 points across the 78 municipalities, and 3 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate. In the same snapshot, Maricao has the highest value for 2020-2024, 60.5% (± 6.8 points), and Juana Díaz the lowest, 7.4% (± 1.3 points).
It says that a household has no internet access. It does not say why, and it does not show speed, price or reliability.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 17.2% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 16.9%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Cabo Rojo goes from 59.90% (2016-2020) to 45.23% (2017-2021). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 85% of barrios and 89% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.

infrastructure.wastewater_permits.plain: How many facilities in each municipality hold their own federal permit to discharge wastewater into a river, a lake or the sea.
infrastructure.wastewater_permits.plain_es: Cuántas instalaciones de cada municipio tienen su propio permiso federal para descargar aguas usadas a un río, un lago o el mar.
infrastructure.wastewater_permits.definition: Facilities with an active individual permit of the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES), which EPA issues in Puerto Rico under the Clean Water Act: sewage treatment plants, water filtration plants, power plants, factories and others that discharge wastewater into surface waters, counted in the municipality that holds the facility's point.
infrastructure.wastewater_permits.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active Clean Water Act facilities of Puerto Rico and downloads eight columns. It keeps the 177 facilities with an individual NPDES permit and leaves out the 1,097 facilities covered by a general permit (construction sites, industrial and municipal stormwater) and the records attached to another permit. Each facility counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 6 of them. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 157 barrios hold one or more.
infrastructure.wastewater_permits.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 177 such facilities in 68 municipalities; the most in Peñuelas 9, Ponce 7, Utuado 7.
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
A permit allows a discharge within limits; holding one is not a violation.
Construction sites and stormwater facilities covered by a general permit are not counted: they come and go with each project.
A facility counts where it stands. The water it discharges flows on to other municipalities downstream.
Septic tanks and discharges with no permit are not in ECHO.
infrastructure.wastewater_permits.source_detail: ECHO cwa_rest_services get_facilities (p_st=PR, p_act=Y) and get_download, columns SourceID, FacFIPSCode, FacLat, FacLong, CWPFacilityTypeIndicator, CWPPermitTypeDesc, CWPMajorMinorStatusFlag, CWPStatus

infrastructure.wastewater_major.plain: How many of the facilities with a wastewater permit EPA classes as major dischargers.
infrastructure.wastewater_major.plain_es: Cuántas de las instalaciones con permiso de aguas usadas la EPA clasifica como descargas mayores.
infrastructure.wastewater_major.definition: Of the facilities with an individual NPDES permit, the ones EPA classes as major (ECHO's major/minor flag): sewage treatment plants built to treat 1 million gallons a day or more, and industrial facilities that EPA scores as major for the volume or the pollutants of their discharge.
infrastructure.wastewater_major.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active Clean Water Act facilities of Puerto Rico and downloads eight columns. It keeps the 177 facilities with an individual NPDES permit and leaves out the 1,097 facilities covered by a general permit (construction sites, industrial and municipal stormwater) and the records attached to another permit. Each facility counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 6 of them. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 60 barrios hold one or more.
infrastructure.wastewater_major.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 62 major dischargers in 49 municipalities; the most in Arecibo 2, Dorado 2, Guayanilla 2.
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
Major is EPA's class for the size or the kind of a discharge, not a finding that the facility pollutes.
A facility counts where it stands; its discharge flows on downstream.

infrastructure.wastewater_plants.plain: How many public sewage treatment plants stand in each municipality.
infrastructure.wastewater_plants.plain_es: Cuántas plantas públicas de tratamiento de aguas usadas hay en cada municipio.
infrastructure.wastewater_plants.definition: Of the facilities with an individual NPDES permit, the publicly owned treatment works (POTW, ECHO's facility type): the plants that treat the sewage of homes and businesses before it is discharged. In Puerto Rico the Aqueduct and Sewer Authority (PRASA) runs nearly all of them.
infrastructure.wastewater_plants.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active Clean Water Act facilities of Puerto Rico and downloads eight columns. It keeps the 177 facilities with an individual NPDES permit and leaves out the 1,097 facilities covered by a general permit (construction sites, industrial and municipal stormwater) and the records attached to another permit. Each facility counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 6 of them. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 51 barrios hold one or more.
infrastructure.wastewater_plants.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 51 plants in 47 municipalities; the most in Caguas 2, Carolina 2, Morovis 2.
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
A plant counts in the municipality where it stands, which may not be the only one it serves; a municipality with no plant can be served by a neighbour's.
The count says nothing about the homes that are not connected to a sewer: a large share of Puerto Rico's homes use septic tanks.
The size of a plant is not given here: one large plant can treat more than many small ones.

infrastructure.wastewater_violation.plain: How many of the facilities with a wastewater permit have a violation of their permit on EPA's record now.
infrastructure.wastewater_violation.plain_es: Cuántas de las instalaciones con permiso de aguas usadas tienen ahora una violación de su permiso en el registro de la EPA.
infrastructure.wastewater_violation.definition: Of the facilities with an individual NPDES permit, the ones whose current compliance status in ECHO is 'Violation Identified' or 'Significant/Category I Noncompliance': a discharge above a permit limit, a missed deadline of a compliance schedule, or a monitoring report that was late or never sent.
infrastructure.wastewater_violation.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active Clean Water Act facilities of Puerto Rico and downloads eight columns. It keeps the 177 facilities with an individual NPDES permit and leaves out the 1,097 facilities covered by a general permit (construction sites, industrial and municipal stormwater) and the records attached to another permit. Each facility counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 6 of them. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept.
infrastructure.wastewater_violation.how_to_read: 113 of Puerto Rico's 177 permitted facilities have a violation on record, 7 of them in significant noncompliance (EPA's most serious class); the most in Barranquitas 4, Cayey 4, Morovis 4.
caveats: A compliance record of the last reported quarter, not a measure of how clean the water is today.
A late or missing report counts the same as a discharge above a limit: the count does not say how serious a violation is. Read a facility's own report on ECHO for what was found.
The status changes every quarter, so the count moves between builds.
Small counts: one facility more or less changes a municipality's value.

facilities.reservoir_history.plain: Each reservoir's water level through time: its range in 2011-2025, its lowest on record, its usual level for each week of the year, every month since its gauge began and the last 400 days.
facilities.reservoir_history.plain_es: El nivel del agua de cada embalse a través del tiempo: su rango en 2011-2025, su nivel más bajo registrado, su nivel usual de cada semana del año, cada mes desde que comenzó su medidor y los últimos 400 días.
facilities.reservoir_history.definition: reservoir_history.json: one record per reservoir (25; 19 in AAA's daily report) with usgs, name, aaa, municipio, geoid, level and level_time (the latest reading at build time), lo and hi with their dates (the lowest and highest daily level in 2011-2025), rec_lo and rec_lo_date (the lowest daily level kept since the gauge began), dropped (daily values left out), wk (53 weeks x 15 years: the mean of each week of the year in each year 2011-2025), m0 and mon (monthly means from m0) and d0 and day (the last 400 daily levels).
facilities.reservoir_history.method: reservoirs.py converts USGS daily values (parameter 72375, feet above local mean sea level) to metres. A month's mean needs 15 days with a value. The history of a gauge starts the year after the last year before 2011 whose median lies more than one 2011-2025 range outside it (another reference, or a reservoir still filling: Toa Vaca reported a depth until 2005, Cerrillos was filling in 1991-1992); after that, a single value more than three ranges below the low or one above the high is left out as a gauge error. The page's 'usual' is the map layer's: the 10th and 90th percentile of the same week's yearly means in 2011-2025, at least 8 years.
facilities.reservoir_history.how_to_read: Open Knowledge › Reservoirs. The ranking orders the reservoirs by the share of the years 2011-2025 with a lower level in the same week; the tanks show where each level sits between its lowest and highest level of 2011-2025, not a volume.
caveats: A level is not a volume: USGS publishes no volumes, and sediment has filled part of several reservoirs.
'Usual' compares a reservoir with its own past (2011-2025), not with AAA's alert levels, which are not published here (no licence stated).
Recent values are provisional, as USGS publishes them.
facilities.reservoir_history.source_detail: USGS Water Data API (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v1): daily (72375) and latest-continuous (72376)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Reservoirs

layers.airports.plain: The airports open to the public and the heliports owned by a public body, as the Federal Aviation Administration lists them every 28 days; private facilities owned privately are counted, not drawn.
layers.airports.plain_es: Los aeropuertos abiertos al público y los helipuertos que son propiedad de una entidad pública, como los lista la Administración Federal de Aviación cada 28 días; las instalaciones privadas de dueños privados se cuentan, pero no se dibujan.
layers.airports.definition: airports.geojson: one point per facility in the FAA's airport data for Puerto Rico (through NTAD) that is open to public use or owned by a public body or the military: 17 in the data in effect on 2026-10-29 (3 airports certificated for airline service, 7 other public-use airports, 7 heliports). Each point has name, type (Airport, Heliport, Seaplane base), municipio, geoid, faa (the FAA identifier), cat (commercial, airport, heliport, seaplane), use (public or private), own (public, private, military, other), elev (feet) and tower (1 when it has an air traffic control tower). The 27 private airports, heliports and seaplane bases owned privately are counted in the notes by kind and never drawn or named.
layers.airports.method: transport_inventories.py reads the NTAD copy of the FAA's facility data for Puerto Rico (no key), keeps the operating facilities, and drops the private-use facilities owned privately: a private heliport can be at a home (docs/transport-inventories.md, sensitive places rule). Airports with an FAA Part 139 certificate are marked as certificated for airline service.
layers.airports.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view. Dark blue: San Juan (Luis Muñoz Marín), Aguadilla (Rafael Hernández) and Ponce (Mercedita), certificated for airline service. Light blue: the other public-use airports, Vieques, Culebra and Ceiba among them. Pink: heliports of hospitals, health centres, the water utility and the Army. Click a point for its FAA identifier, owner, use, elevation and tower.
caveats: Private airports, heliports and seaplane bases owned privately (27 in October 2026) are counted in the note but not drawn.
The Stations, terminals and airports layer shows airports too, from the same FAA list and OpenStreetMap.
layers.airports.geography: Points in the municipios that have one
layers.airports.source_detail: NTAD Aviation Facilities (layer 0): EFF_DATE, SITE_TYPE_CODE, ARPT_ID, ARPT_NAME, OWNERSHIP_TYPE_CODE, FACILITY_USE_CODE, LAT_DECIMAL, LONG_DECIMAL, ELEV, ARPT_STATUS, FAR_139_TYPE_CODE, TWR_TYPE_CODE

3D view, Layers tab: Airports and heliports

layers.ferries.plain: The three ferry crossings of Puerto Rico (San Juan to Cataño, Ceiba to Vieques and Ceiba to Culebra), wider where more passengers travelled in the newest National Census of Ferry Operators.
layers.ferries.plain_es: Los tres cruces en lancha de Puerto Rico (San Juan a Cataño, Ceiba a Vieques y Ceiba a Culebra), más anchos donde viajaron más pasajeros según el censo nacional de operadores de lanchas más reciente.
layers.ferries.definition: ferry_routes.geojson: one line per pair of terminals with a line in NTAD (3), with name, type, pax (passengers in the census's data year, both directions added), veh (vehicles), trips (trips a year, both directions) and min (minutes a crossing, the average of the two directions). Census of 2024, data year 2024: 1,616,045 passengers on the three crossings. Culebra–Vieques (234 passengers in 2024) has no line in NTAD and is counted in the notes, not drawn.
layers.ferries.method: transport_inventories.py reads the newest census on data.bts.gov (the same files gateway_series.py counts by municipio): terminals, segments and the operators' figures for each one-way segment. It adds the two directions of each crossing and draws it with the line NTAD's ferry routes give for that pair of terminals (same terminal ids), simplified to about 20 m.
layers.ferries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view. Ceiba–Vieques carried 641,183 passengers in 2024 and Ceiba–Culebra 546,258, with about 40,000 vehicles each; San Juan–Cataño carried 428,604 passengers and no vehicles. Click a line for its trips and the time of a crossing.
caveats: The census is every two years and reports a year of operation, not today's service; the timetabled ferry trips of today are on the Transit routes layer.
The operator reports the figures; they are not audited counts.
layers.ferries.source_detail: NCFO 2024 on data.bts.gov (terminals difu-6bgs, segments 2ygc-ds4z, operator segments 7umd-qc2k): passengers, vehicles, trips_per_year, average_trip_time; NTAD Ferry Routes (seg_terminal1_id, seg_terminal2_id, line).
