route_compare.minutes_midday.plain: The median time the timetable gives the main stop pattern, first to last stop, for trips leaving from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.
route_compare.minutes_midday.plain_es: La mediana del tiempo que el horario da al patrón principal, de la primera a la última parada, en los viajes que salen de 10:00 a.m. a 2:00 p.m.
route_compare.minutes_midday.definition: Median scheduled time from first to last stop of the main pattern's trips starting 10:00-14:00, in minutes to one decimal. Blank when none.
route_compare.minutes_midday.geography: Each bus route of the Route analysis (97 routes of 12 systems)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Route analysis, route comparison

route_compare.minutes_peak.plain: The median time the timetable gives the main stop pattern, first to last stop, for trips leaving from 6:00 to 9:00 a.m.
route_compare.minutes_peak.plain_es: La mediana del tiempo que el horario da al patrón principal, de la primera a la última parada, en los viajes que salen de 6:00 a 9:00 a.m.
route_compare.minutes_peak.definition: Median scheduled time from first to last stop of the main pattern's trips starting 6:00-9:00, in minutes to one decimal. Blank when none.
route_compare.minutes_peak.method: transit_runtime.csv (from the road-features analysis's transit_exposure.py), the row of the route's main pattern.
route_compare.minutes_peak.geography: Each bus route of the Route analysis (97 routes of 12 systems)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Route analysis, route comparison

route_compare.speed_kmh.plain: The average speed the timetable plans for the route's main stop pattern, from its first to its last timed stop.
route_compare.speed_kmh.plain_es: La velocidad promedio que el horario planifica para el patrón principal de la ruta, de su primera a su última parada con hora.
route_compare.speed_kmh.definition: Length of the timed path divided by the median scheduled time from first to last stop of the main pattern's trips, in km/h. Blank for a timetable-only route whose timed path is under half its route line (the timed stretch is not the whole trip).
route_compare.speed_kmh.method: route_compare.py: path_km / (median run / 3600); set blank when timepoints_only and path_km < 0.5 x line length.
caveats: Scheduled, not observed.
A timetable with long waits at stops gives a low speed.
Marked with an asterisk on the page for timetable-only routes: the speed of the stretch between their two timed stops.
route_compare.speed_kmh.geography: Each bus route of the Route analysis (97 routes of 12 systems)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Route analysis, route comparison

route_compare.stops.plain: How many distinct stops the route uses.
route_compare.stops.plain_es: Cuántas paradas distintas usa la ruta.
route_compare.stops.definition: Distinct stop ids of every stop pattern of the route in trips.json, plus the stops transport.json lists for the route (so a timetable-only route counts all its stops, not only the two timed ones).
route_compare.stops.geography: Each bus route of the Route analysis (97 routes of 12 systems)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Route analysis, route comparison

route_compare.operator.plain: The short id of the transit system that runs the route, the same id the observatory's other transit files use.
route_compare.operator.plain_es: El identificador corto del sistema de transporte que opera la ruta, el mismo que usan los otros archivos de transporte del observatorio.
route_compare.operator.definition: Operator id of the GTFS feed: ati, san_juan, bayamon, guaynabo, caguas, canovanas, fajardo, humacao, juncos, san_lorenzo, patillas, vieques. It is a field of both tables (routes and operators) and joins them.
route_compare.operator.method: The id the build gives each feed (transport.py), copied from trips.json.
route_compare.operator.geography: Each bus route of the Route analysis (97 routes of 12 systems)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Route analysis, route comparison

route_compare.operator_name.plain: The name of the transit system as the page shows it.
route_compare.operator_name.plain_es: El nombre del sistema de transporte como lo muestra la página.
route_compare.operator_name.definition: The display name of the operator (ATI (AMA), San Juan, Bayamón, ...). A field of both tables.
route_compare.operator_name.geography: Each bus route of the Route analysis (97 routes of 12 systems)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Route analysis, route comparison

route_compare.feed_end.plain: The last day the system's published timetable covers.
route_compare.feed_end.plain_es: El último día que cubre el horario publicado del sistema.
route_compare.feed_end.definition: The end date of the operator's GTFS feed (its calendar's last service day), as transport.json gives it. Field of the operators table.
route_compare.feed_end.method: route_compare.py: feed_end of the operator's stops in transport.json.
route_compare.feed_end.geography: Each bus route of the Route analysis (97 routes of 12 systems)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Route analysis, route comparison

route_compare.timepoints_only.plain: Whether the route's timetable gives a time only at the first and the last stop of each trip.
route_compare.timepoints_only.plain_es: Si el horario de la ruta da la hora solo en la primera y la última parada de cada viaje.
route_compare.timepoints_only.definition: true when the main stop pattern of trips.json has two stops or fewer: every route of Bayamón, Caguas, Juncos and San Lorenzo, and ATI express route 20 (two stops). Their length, speed and crossings come from the operator's route line.
caveats: On the page, the length, speed and crossings of these routes carry an asterisk.
route_compare.timepoints_only.geography: Each bus route of the Route analysis (97 routes of 12 systems)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Route analysis, route comparison

route_compare.weekday_trips.plain: How many trips the route makes on a typical weekday, both directions added.
route_compare.weekday_trips.plain_es: Cuántos viajes hace la ruta en un día de semana típico, sumadas las dos direcciones.
route_compare.weekday_trips.definition: Number of bus trips of the operator and route label in trips.json (a typical Wednesday).
route_compare.weekday_trips.method: Count of trips.json trips with the route's operator and label and mode bus.
route_compare.weekday_trips.geography: Each bus route of the Route analysis (97 routes of 12 systems)

view.label: Knowledge Area: Route analysis, route comparison

measures.route_connections.plain: Two checks: whether the start and the end are within 300 m of a scheduled stop, and how many scheduled stops lie within 250 m of the route, by operator.
measures.route_connections.plain_es: Dos verificaciones: si el origen y el destino están a 300 m o menos de una parada con horario, y cuántas paradas con horario hay a 250 m o menos de la ruta, por operador.
measures.route_connections.definition: Start and End: the scheduled stop nearest to the first and to the last point you chose, if one lies within 300 m in a straight line. The card shows the stop name, its operator and the distance in metres, or 'no scheduled stop within 300 m'. Existing stops within 250 m of the route: the number of scheduled stops within 250 m of the route line, grouped by operator. A scheduled stop is a stop in a public timetable feed (GTFS, the General Transit Feed Specification) from ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or from a municipal system.
measures.route_connections.method: plan.js looks at the scheduled stops in the transit features file. For the first and last chosen points it keeps the nearest stop within 300 m. For the route line it counts the stops within 250 m of the simplified line and groups them by operator's short name.
measures.route_connections.how_to_read: Use it to see where a new route could join an existing one. A stop near the end is a place to connect, not proof that a rider can transfer.
caveats: Only the first and last points are tested. Points you add between them are not.
Stops of operators whose timetables have expired are counted.
It does not say whether the lines at that stop go where you need, or how often.
The distance from an end is measured from the point you chose, not from the road it is snapped to.
measures.route_connections.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)
measures.route_connections.source_detail: transport.json (stops from ATI and municipal feeds); operators.json (operator names); site/js/plan.js (score, endTxt)

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)
Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example with no overlap: Mayagüez to Aguadilla)

measures.distance_rules.plain: The route planner and the Transit tab use a few fixed distances, all in a straight line: 150, 250, 300, 400, 500 and 800 metres. This entry says what each is for.
measures.distance_rules.plain_es: El planificador de rutas y la pestaña "Transporte" usan unas pocas distancias fijas, todas en línea recta: 150, 250, 300, 400, 500 y 800 metros. Esta entrada explica para qué sirve cada una.
measures.distance_rules.definition: Each distance is a setting chosen for this tool. 400 m (about a quarter mile) is a common rule of thumb for walking access to a stop. Check any agency's or programme's own definition before comparing. All are straight-line distances calculated with a flat-earth approximation, not walking distances along streets.
measures.distance_rules.method: The route planner (plan.js) and the road router (roads.js) compute distances in the browser from longitude and latitude with a flat-earth approximation: 111,320 m per degree of longitude at the equator, scaled by the cosine of the latitude, and 110,574 m per degree of latitude. The distance from each census block to its nearest scheduled stop (the basis of the 400 m and 800 m rules) and the 250 m integration-point test are computed at build time by network.py with a similar formula: 111,320 m per degree of latitude, and the same figure scaled by the cosine of the latitude for longitude. North-south distances in the build are therefore up to about 0.7% longer than in the browser. network.js and plan.js read those stored results: network.js applies the 800 m test to them and plan.js applies the 400 m test when it counts residents with no stop near a route.
measures.distance_rules.how_to_read: Read each distance as a catchment around a line or a stop. A longer distance includes more people and places and says less about how easy it is to reach them.
caveats: A straight line ignores rivers, hills, fences and the street pattern.
The 400 m walking distance is about a quarter mile. The 800 m distance for service gaps is about half a mile.

values.12 m: Tolerance for simplifying the route line before it is measured.
values.100 m, 250 m, 500 m: Spacing of sample points along the route: up to 30 km, over 30 up to 100 km, over 100 km.
values.150 m: A route 'runs alongside' an existing route when a published line is within 150 m of a sample point.
values.250 m: Scheduled stops within 250 m of the route are counted. Stops of two operators within 250 m of each other make an integration point.
values.300 m: Connections at the ends: the nearest scheduled stop to the first or last point, if within 300 m.
values.400 m: Residents and tourism places counted near the route. Residents counted as served when a scheduled stop is within 400 m. The test for 'no scheduled stop within 400 m'.
values.500 m: Snap radius from a chosen point to a road.
values.800 m: Service gap: a block whose nearest scheduled stop is more than 800 m away.

measures.distance_rules.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

measures.route_sampling.plain: The flood, protected-area, overlap and municipality measures check points along the route, not the whole line. The spacing depends on the route's length.
measures.route_sampling.plain_es: Las medidas de inundación, áreas protegidas, coincidencia con otras rutas y municipios revisan puntos a lo largo de la ruta, no la línea completa. La distancia entre los puntos depende del largo de la ruta.
measures.route_sampling.definition: The route line is simplified to a 12 m tolerance. Points are then placed along it every 100 m for routes up to 30 km, every 250 m for routes over 30 km and up to 100 km, and every 500 m for longer routes. Every straight piece of the simplified line gets at least one point. The overlap, flood and protected-area measures are each the share of sample points that meet their test, rounded to a whole percent. The municipalities measure is the number of different municipalities that contain at least one sample point.
measures.route_sampling.method: plan.js applies Douglas-Peucker simplification (a method that drops points that lie close to a straight line between their neighbours) with a 12 m tolerance, then calls samples() with a step of 100, 250 or 500 m chosen from the route length.
measures.route_sampling.how_to_read: A percentage is a share of points, not a share of kilometres. Short features between points can be missed.
caveats: A curvy stretch has many short pieces, each with at least one point, so it weighs a little more than a straight stretch of the same length.
Residents, tourism places and stops use the distance to the line, not these points.
measures.route_sampling.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

measures.route_time.plain: A rough driving time for the route, in minutes, at fixed planning speeds by road class. It leaves out stops, traffic and waiting. Use it to compare routes, not as a bus timetable.
measures.route_time.plain_es: Un tiempo aproximado de manejo para la ruta, en minutos, a velocidades fijas de planificación según la clase de carretera. No incluye paradas, tráfico ni esperas. Sirve para comparar rutas, no como horario de guaguas.
measures.route_time.definition: The sum over legs of the time at planning speeds. On a leg that follows roads: the time along each road piece (its length divided by the speed of its road class), plus the straight-line gap between each chosen point and its road, counted at walking pace (1.4 m/s). On a leg that cannot follow roads: its straight-line length at 8 m/s (28.8 km/h). Shown as '~N min', rounded to whole minutes, at least 1.
measures.route_time.method: roads.js adds the seconds of every leg. plan.js shows the total only when Follow roads is on and at least one leg follows roads; otherwise it shows a dash. In the list of legs, minutes appear only for legs that follow roads.
measures.route_time.how_to_read: The number is the time at these planning speeds, for example 25 km/h on residential streets and 90 km/h on motorways. It is closer to a free-flow driving time than to a bus timetable: in the example (snapshot 2026-10, Río Piedras to Caguas) the average speed is about 76 km/h (24.3 km in about 19 min). A real bus trip is longer: it has stops, boarding, signals and traffic. Use the number only to compare routes.
caveats: The speeds are planning values by road class, not observed or posted speeds.
When some legs cannot follow roads, the total time still includes them, as straight lines at 8 m/s (28.8 km/h). The list of legs shows minutes only for legs that follow roads.
The time is not a prediction of a real service and does not depend on the day or the hour.
measures.route_time.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

measures.route_municipalities.plain: How many municipalities the planned route passes through. The card lists the first four names and then says 'and N more'.
measures.route_municipalities.plain_es: Por cuántos municipios pasa la ruta planificada. La tarjeta da los primeros cuatro nombres y luego dice "y N más".
measures.route_municipalities.definition: The number of different municipalities whose boundary contains at least one sample point of the route, with their names.
measures.route_municipalities.method: plan.js finds, for each sample point, the municipality polygon that contains it and collects the distinct names. See the entry on how the route is sampled.
measures.route_municipalities.how_to_read: Use it to see which local governments a route involves. A route that only grazes a municipality can be missed.
caveats: A municipality touched between two sample points (100 to 500 m apart) is not counted.
The boundaries follow the shoreline, so a sample point on a bridge or offshore can belong to no municipality.
The boundaries are simplified by about 22 m (0.0002 degree), so a sample point near a boundary can be assigned to the neighbouring municipality.
measures.route_municipalities.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)
measures.route_municipalities.source_detail: municipios.geojson: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County MapServer layer 11 (Counties 500K, shoreline-clipped); site/js/plan.js (score)

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

measures.route_residents.plain: How many people live in census blocks whose point is within 400 metres of the planned route. It shows who lives near the line, not who would ride it.
measures.route_residents.plain_es: Cuántas personas viven en bloques censales cuyo punto está a 400 metros o menos de la ruta planificada. Muestra quién vive cerca de la línea, no quién la usaría.
measures.route_residents.definition: The sum of the 2020 Census resident counts of every census block with residents whose internal point lies within 400 m (straight line) of the route line. A block counts whole when its point qualifies. Blocks are not split.
measures.route_residents.method: population_blocks.json lists, for every block with residents, its longitude and latitude (the Census internal point, rounded to 4 decimals), its residents and its distance to the nearest scheduled stop. plan.js simplifies the route line to a 12 m tolerance and adds the residents of each block whose point is within 400 m of any piece of it.
measures.route_residents.how_to_read: Use it as a catchment: the number of people close to the line. It is not ridership or demand.
caveats: The distance is in a straight line, not along streets. A person can be within 400 m and still face a long walk.
A block is counted whole or not at all. A large block whose point is farther than 400 m is left out even if part of it is near.
The counts are from April 2020 and have not been updated.
400 m is about a quarter mile, the walking distance the observatory uses for access to a stop.
measures.route_residents.geography: Census blocks of Puerto Rico (36,570 blocks have residents in the 2020 Census)
measures.route_residents.source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 10 (2020 Census blocks), fields POP100, INTPTLAT, INTPTLON; site/js/plan.js (score)

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

measures.route_residents_unserved.plain: Of the people who live within 400 m of the route, how many live more than 400 m from every scheduled stop in the observatory's data. These people have no scheduled stop near them.
measures.route_residents_unserved.plain_es: De las personas que viven a 400 m o menos de la ruta, cuántas viven a más de 400 m de todas las paradas con horario en los datos del observatorio. Estas personas no tienen una parada con horario cerca.
measures.route_residents_unserved.definition: Residents counted in 'Residents within 400 m of the route' whose census block has its nearest scheduled stop more than 400 m away (straight line). A scheduled stop is a stop in a public timetable feed (GTFS, the General Transit Feed Specification) from ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or from a municipal system. The result card calls them 'of them have no scheduled stop within 400 m today'.
measures.route_residents_unserved.method: population_blocks.json gives each block's distance in metres to its nearest scheduled stop, capped at 9,999. plan.js adds the residents of the blocks near the route whose distance is above 400. The distances are recomputed by the transit refresh.
measures.route_residents_unserved.how_to_read: Compare it with 'Residents within 400 m of the route'. A high share means the route passes many people who have no stop nearby today. The distances were last computed on 2026-10-02.
caveats: 'Today' means the build or refresh date. Stops of operators whose timetables have expired still count as stops, so the true number with no service now is larger.
Only stops in public timetable feeds count. Routes that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap have no stops here, so público service is not counted as service.
A stop within 400 m says that a stop exists. It does not say how often vehicles come or when.
The distance is in a straight line, not along streets.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

measures.route_length.plain: How long the planned route is, in kilometres, along the roads it follows. The label under the number says 'by road', 'partly by road' or 'straight line'.
measures.route_length.plain_es: Cuánto mide la ruta planificada, en kilómetros, por las carreteras que sigue. La etiqueta debajo del número dice "por carretera", "en parte por carretera" o "en línea recta".
measures.route_length.definition: The sum of the lengths of all legs between the points you chose (From, any added stops and To; 8 points at most). A leg that follows roads counts the length of its road path plus the straight-line gap from each chosen point to the nearest point on a road. A leg that cannot follow roads counts its straight-line length.
measures.route_length.method: roads.js finds the fastest road path for each leg and measures the drawn line with a flat-earth approximation. plan.js adds the legs. With more than one leg, the card also lists each leg with its length and, for legs on roads, its minutes. The label is 'by road' when every leg follows roads, 'partly by road' when some do not, and 'straight line' when Follow roads is switched off.
measures.route_length.how_to_read: It is the length of the path the planner drew, not a measured distance on the ground. It is not the fastest or shortest real bus route.
caveats: A leg that cannot follow roads, for example a leg to another island, counts at its straight-line length, so it can be much shorter than any real trip by sea or air.
If the road file cannot be loaded, the route is drawn as straight lines and a note under the numbers says so.
In the GeoJSON download the same number is called length_km and has two decimals.
The points you choose are stored in the page address (after #r=) to about 11 m. A shared link shares them. Do not choose a home address if you plan to share the link.
measures.route_length.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)
measures.route_length.source_detail: site/js/roads.js (path) and site/js/plan.js (renderResult); roads.bin from OpenStreetMap

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

measures.route_flood.plain: The share of the planned route that crosses areas the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps as high-risk for flooding, which have a 1% chance of flooding in any year. The card turns amber above 20%.
measures.route_flood.plain_es: La proporción de la ruta planificada que cruza áreas que FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) marca como de alto riesgo de inundación, que tienen 1% de probabilidad de inundarse en cualquier año. La tarjeta se pone ámbar por encima del 20%.
measures.route_flood.definition: The share of the route's sample points that fall inside a polygon of the National Flood Hazard Layer of FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency) flagged as a Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA_TF = T), rounded to a whole percent. In the published file these are zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99 and VE. Zone X and zone D are not counted.
measures.route_flood.method: plan.js tests each sample point against the polygons of the flood file with a point-in-polygon test (checking whether the point lies inside the polygon). See the entry on how the route is sampled.
measures.route_flood.how_to_read: A high value means much of the route lies in mapped flood hazard. It does not say how deep water would get or whether the road is raised.
caveats: The flood polygons are simplified by about 5 m for display, so points near a boundary can be misplaced.
It is a share of sample points, not of length.
The map shows hazard at a point. It does not describe bridges, culverts or the road surface.
The 20% amber threshold is this tool's own choice, not a standard.
measures.route_flood.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)
measures.route_flood.source_detail: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 (flood.geojson, field SFHA_TF); site/js/plan.js (score)

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

measures.route_protected.plain: The share of the planned route that passes through protected areas in the USGS Protected Areas Database. The card shows it only when it is above 0%.
measures.route_protected.plain_es: La proporción de la ruta planificada que pasa por áreas protegidas de la base de datos de áreas protegidas del USGS (Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos). La tarjeta la muestra solo cuando es mayor de 0%.
measures.route_protected.definition: The share of the route's sample points that fall inside any polygon of the protected-areas file (USGS, the United States Geological Survey), rounded to a whole percent. Every designation is counted, including the proclamation boundaries (PROC) such as El Yunque National Forest and the Culebra and Vieques National Wildlife Refuges.
measures.route_protected.method: plan.js tests each sample point against the polygons of the protected-areas file with a point-in-polygon test (checking whether the point lies inside the polygon). See the entry on how the route is sampled.
measures.route_protected.how_to_read: A value above 0 means the route runs through land with a protected designation. It does not say that the road is closed or that the land is off limits. In the 2026-10 snapshot the protected-areas file has seven proclamation boundaries.
caveats: The statistic for tourism places leaves out the proclamation boundaries (seven records in the 2026-10 snapshot); this route measure counts them, so the two are not on the same basis.
The file includes areas with different levels of protection and public access. The share does not tell them apart.
It is a share of sample points, not of length.
measures.route_protected.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

measures.route_overlap.plain: The share of the planned route within 150 m of a published transit route; a high share means the route mostly repeats lines that exist. The card turns amber above 50%, a threshold this tool chose.
measures.route_overlap.plain_es: La proporción de la ruta planificada que queda a 150 m o menos de una ruta de transporte colectivo publicada; una proporción alta significa que la ruta repite mayormente líneas que ya existen. La tarjeta se pone ámbar por encima del 50%, un límite que escogió esta herramienta.
measures.route_overlap.definition: The share of the route's sample points that have a published route line within 150 m, rounded to a whole percent. Routes that volunteers mapped only in OpenStreetMap (públicos) and ferry routes are not counted. Routes of every other operator are counted, including the Tren Urbano rail line.
measures.route_overlap.method: plan.js indexes every segment of the published route lines in grid cells of 0.002 degree (about 220 m) and tests each sample point against the segments in its own and the neighbouring cells. See the entry on how the route is sampled.
measures.route_overlap.how_to_read: 100% means the route follows existing lines for its whole length. 0% means no line from an ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or municipal timetable feed is near. Públicos mapped in OpenStreetMap and ferries are not counted. It says nothing about stops or how often vehicles run.
caveats: Lines of operators whose timetables have expired are counted.
A route can run beside a line and still have no stop near it. The measure compares lines, not stops.
It is a share of sample points, not of length. See the entry on sampling.
The 50% amber threshold is this tool's own choice, not a standard.
measures.route_overlap.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)
measures.route_overlap.source_detail: transit_routes.geojson (all operators except 'osm' and ferries); site/js/plan.js (segments, score)

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)
Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example with no overlap: Mayagüez to Aguadilla)

measures.route_tourism_places.plain: How many tourism places lie within 400 m of the planned route, and how many of them are lodgings. Tourism places are Attractions, Gastronomy (restaurants, bars and cafes), Accommodations and Visitor services.
measures.route_tourism_places.plain_es: Cuántos lugares turísticos hay a 400 m o menos de la ruta planificada, y cuántos de ellos son alojamientos. Los lugares turísticos son "Atracciones", "Gastronomía" (restaurantes, bares y cafés), "Alojamientos" y "Servicios para visitantes".
measures.route_tourism_places.definition: The number of listings in the places file with an Overture confidence of at least 0.5, other than places of worship, whose point lies within 400 m (straight line) of the route line. Lodgings are the places in the Accommodations category (the route card calls them lodgings).
measures.route_tourism_places.method: plan.js goes through the places file, skips places of worship and listings below 0.5 confidence, and counts those within 400 m of the simplified route line. It counts the lodgings separately.
measures.route_tourism_places.how_to_read: It says how many visitor places the route passes. A place is a listing, not a verified business.
caveats: The same 0.5 confidence rule as the map statistics applies. The map's own filters (categories, confidence slider) do not change this count.
Listings can be closed, moved or missing.
The distance is in a straight line, not along streets.

Lodgings are listings the observatory's rules file under hotels, resorts, inns, guest houses, hostels, campgrounds and vacation properties (categories such as vacation rental, villa, cottage, cabin, holiday and condo), or under Overture's lodging group. They are Overture listings, not a lodging register.
measures.route_tourism_places.geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)
measures.route_tourism_places.source_detail: Overture Maps Places, release 2026-09-23.1, classified by build.py; site/js/plan.js (score)

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

transit.route_first_last.plain: The earliest and the latest time a weekday trip on the route starts, in seconds after midnight. The map shows them as clock times.
transit.route_first_last.plain_es: La hora más temprana y la más tarde en que sale un viaje de lunes a viernes en la ruta, en segundos después de la medianoche. El mapa las muestra como horas del reloj.
transit.route_first_last.definition: first is the earliest and last is the latest departure from the first stop of any weekday trip on the route. Seconds after midnight, local time (12600 is 03:30). In the 2026-10 snapshot it is present for 149 routes; first runs from 12600 (03:30) to 29700 (08:15) and last from 39600 (11:00) to 84600 (23:30). It is null for the 16 OpenStreetMap (OSM) routes.
transit.route_first_last.method: network.py sorts the time at the first stop of each weekday trip and keeps the smallest and the largest.
transit.route_first_last.how_to_read: Divide by 3600 to get hours. last is when the final trip leaves its first stop, not when it arrives. A timetable covers the dates from the operator's feed.start to feed.end in operators.json, not the build date. In the build of 2026-10-02 the earliest start is 2023-01-01 and the latest end is 2029-12-31; Ponce's feed ended 2024-12-31. Cite both the build date and the feed dates.
caveats: For Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and Guaynabo, which list each direction, the two values mix both directions of travel; in the 2026-10 snapshot the other 23 feeds do not separate directions.
They are taken from the stop times as listed, so in the 2026-10 snapshot the five Patillas routes with an inferred stop order also show them even though their times are not used in the replay.
transit.route_first_last.source_detail: GTFS stop_times.txt (time at the first stop of each weekday trip), joined to trips.txt and calendar.txt

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Transit routes

transit.route_drawing.plain: A route line is the operator's own shape when the feed has one, otherwise a path along roads between the stops. If the stop order looks wrong the observatory infers one, and if nothing works it joins the stops with straight dotted lines.
transit.route_drawing.plain_es: La línea de una ruta es la forma del propio operador cuando la fuente de horarios la trae; si no, es un camino por las carreteras entre las paradas. Si el orden de las paradas parece incorrecto, el observatorio deduce uno, y si nada funciona, une las paradas con líneas rectas punteadas.
transit.route_drawing.definition: The counts below are for the 2026-10 snapshot. 1. Feed shape: if the feed lists a route shape (the line the operator publishes for the path of a route), the observatory keeps up to the two most used shapes of the route (usually one per direction). 50 routes are drawn this way, including every Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) route. 2. Road-snapped: with no shape, the observatory takes the stops of the longest trip in each direction and links each pair of neighbouring stops by the fastest road path in the OpenStreetMap road network (roads.bin). 94 routes are drawn this way. 3. Inferred order: if a feed lists its stops out of travel order, the observatory picks a plausible order and then snaps it to roads. 5 routes are drawn this way, all from Patillas. 4. Straight dotted: if too little of a route can be snapped, the stops are joined by straight lines and drawn dotted. No route uses this in the 2026-10 snapshot. 5. OpenStreetMap: the 16 públicos and trolley routes are drawn from the lines volunteers mapped.
transit.route_drawing.method: Road snapping: each stop is moved to the nearest road within 500 m; a leg is accepted if the road path is no longer than 3 times the straight distance plus 400 m; stops less than 25 m apart are joined directly. A route is kept as road-snapped only if at least 60% of the legs in each direction follow a road; otherwise it falls back to straight lines. The line is then simplified (tolerance about 3 m). Inferred order: a feed is flagged when the stop order has a zig-zag ratio above 2.5 (the length of the path through the stops in listed order divided by the length of a nearest-neighbour tour; real routes sit near 1 to 2) or when the stop names are in alphabetical order. The order is then rebuilt from the terminal or first stop by always going to the nearest unvisited stop by road, improved by reversing stretches of the order while that shortens the road distance, and the line returns to its start; for more than 45 distinct stops the order is not rebuilt and the route falls back to straight lines. A route whose stops did not change keeps its previous line (see the entry on the route line fingerprint).
transit.route_drawing.how_to_read: On the map a solid line follows the operator's shape or the roads, a lighter dashed line is a route with inferred stop order, a dotted line joins stops straight, and a gold dashed line is an OpenStreetMap route. Ferries are dashed teal.
caveats: Only a feed shape is the operator's own alignment. A road-snapped line is an estimate and the real street may differ.
A route with an inferred order shows a plausible path, not the route the operator runs. Its times are left out of the timetable replay.
The feed's route colour is not used on the map; line colour follows the mode and the type of operator.
Road-snapped lines are derived from OpenStreetMap roads, which are under the Open Database License. Credit OpenStreetMap contributors and check the license terms before reuse.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Transit routes

transit.route_geometry_source.plain: Says whether the line is the operator's own shape, a path along roads, a path along roads with a guessed stop order, or a volunteer-mapped line.
transit.route_geometry_source.plain_es: Dice si la línea es la forma del propio operador, un camino por las carreteras, un camino por las carreteras con un orden de paradas deducido o una línea mapeada por personas voluntarias.
transit.route_geometry_source.definition: A code for how the line of a route from Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), a municipality or OpenStreetMap was made. The code stops (a straight dotted line joining the stops) exists in the program but no route uses it in the 2026-10 snapshot.
transit.route_geometry_source.method: Set by network.py (shape, stops), snap_routes (roads, roads_inferred) and load_osm_routes (osm). See How route lines are drawn.
transit.route_geometry_source.how_to_read: Trust shape most. Treat roads as a good estimate, roads_inferred as a rough guess, and osm as a volunteer map.
caveats: The code stops would appear as a dotted straight line; none is present in the 2026-10 snapshot.

values.shape: The route shape published in the feed. 50 routes in the 2026-10 snapshot (all ATI routes and 12 municipal ones).
values.roads: No shape in the feed; the line follows roads between the stops in listed order. 94 routes in the 2026-10 snapshot.
values.roads_inferred: The feed lists the stops out of travel order, so the order of visit is inferred and the line follows roads. 5 routes (Patillas) in the 2026-10 snapshot.
values.osm: Line mapped by volunteers in OpenStreetMap. 16 routes in the 2026-10 snapshot.

transit.route_geometry_source.source_detail: GTFS shapes.txt (shape); the OpenStreetMap road network, Geofabrik Puerto Rico extract (roads.bin), for roads and roads_inferred; OpenStreetMap route relations (osm)

transit.route_network.plain: The name of the network or operator that volunteers wrote on an OpenStreetMap (OSM) route, such as Carros Públicos. Only OSM routes can have it.
transit.route_network.plain_es: El nombre de la red o del operador que personas voluntarias escribieron en una ruta de OpenStreetMap (OSM), como Carros Públicos. Solo lo pueden tener las rutas de OSM.
transit.route_network.definition: Text of the OSM network tag, or the operator tag when there is no network. The key is present only on OSM routes: in the 2026-10 snapshot on all 16, with a null value on 4 of them. It is absent from feed routes.
transit.route_network.method: Copied from the OSM tags by load_osm_routes.
caveats: The text is free and unchecked. It is not an official operator name.

values.Carros Públicos: 9 routes in the 2026-10 snapshot, all labelled Público.

transit.route_network.source_detail: OpenStreetMap route relation tags network, then operator

transit.route_order_note.plain: A sentence that explains why the observatory had to guess the order of a route's stops. In the 2026-10 snapshot it appears on five Patillas routes.
transit.route_order_note.plain_es: Una oración que explica por qué el observatorio tuvo que deducir el orden de las paradas de una ruta. En el corte de datos de 2026-10 aparece en cinco rutas de Patillas.
transit.route_order_note.definition: Text, present only on routes whose feed lists the stops out of travel order. It states the zig-zag ratio found and that the order of visit is inferred and the times are not usable. The sentence says alphabetically when the stop names are in alphabetical order, and out of travel order otherwise. In the 2026-10 snapshot the five notes give the ratios 2.72, 2.77, 2.93, 4.44 and 4.99, and all five say out of travel order.
transit.route_order_note.method: Written by snap_routes in network.py when order_quality flags a route (zig-zag ratio above 2.5, or at least 5 stops in alphabetical order).
transit.route_order_note.how_to_read: When a note is present, read the line as a plausible path, not the real route.
caveats: Trip counts and first and last times for these routes are still in the file. Their times are left out of the timetable replay files.
transit.route_order_note.source_detail: Computed by network.py from the stop order in GTFS stop_times.txt and the stop names in stops.txt

transit.route_operator.plain: The id of the operator that publishes the route: ati, a municipality's id, or osm for volunteer-mapped routes.
transit.route_operator.plain_es: El identificador del operador que publica la ruta: ati, el identificador de un municipio u osm para las rutas mapeadas por personas voluntarias.
transit.route_operator.definition: Operator id, the same id used in operators.json and in the operator field of scheduled stops. In the 2026-10 snapshot there are 26 different values among 165 routes; osm marks the 16 OpenStreetMap routes.
transit.route_operator.method: Set by network.py for each feed.
transit.route_operator.how_to_read: Join to operators.json by id to find the feed status and dates.
caveats: An operator id is a short label made by the observatory from the municipality name; it is not an official code.
