municipalities.pop_walk_active_pct.plain: Out of every 100 residents, how many live within a 400 m walk, along mapped roads, of a scheduled stop whose operator's timetable has not ended. It is the observatory's main measure of residents' access to transit.
municipalities.pop_walk_active_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 residentes, cuántos viven a 400 m o menos a pie, por las calles mapeadas, de una parada con horario cuyo operador no ha dejado vencer su horario. Es la medida principal del observatorio del acceso de los residentes al transporte colectivo.
municipalities.pop_walk_active_pct.definition: Residents (2020 Census) whose block is a walk of 400 m or less, along mapped roads, from a scheduled stop of an operator whose feed is active (not expired on the build date of the transit data), divided by all residents of the municipality, times 100, rounded to one decimal. It is pop_served_active_pct measured by walking instead of a straight line, and it equals the exposure series' walk_cur for the municipio.
municipalities.pop_walk_active_pct.method: Same blocks and walking rule as pop_walk_pct, but only stops of operators whose feed status is not expired count. See pop_walk_400m.
municipalities.pop_walk_active_pct.how_to_read: A high value means most people live a short walk from a stop with a timetable in force. In the 2026-10 snapshot the value is 12.3% island-wide (403,421 residents), against 22.2% in a straight line, and ranges from 0.0 to 50.0 (San Juan). 50 of the 78 municipalities have 0.0 and 70 are under 25%. The largest drops from the straight line are Guaynabo (77.8% to 43.3%), San Juan (80.9% to 50.0%), Vega Alta and Carolina (58.1% to 32.2%). The map's Municipality tab shows it as 'of residents within a 400 m walk of a stop with a current timetable' and highlights values under 25%. It is the Overview's headline for Mobility.
caveats: Along mapped roads, not every way a person can walk. The road file has no footways, paths, steps, sidewalks or crossings. On 2026-10-16 the same count on the full OpenStreetMap walking network (footways, paths and service roads included) gave 15.5% of residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop, against 15.6% on roads.bin, and municipal shares moved a median 0.0 points (largest 1.7, Carolina).

Each block joins the network at the road nearest its internal point. A large block (a housing complex, a condominium) that fronts an avenue on one side but lies nearer a back street reads a longer walk than its residents may make. Joining each block also to every road within 60 m raises the island share from 15.5% to 17.1% (within 100 m: 19.1%), still far below the straight line (28.2%). Read the share as a careful estimate, with about that range around it.

13.9% of residents (455,383, in 4,002 blocks) live in blocks with no walkable road within 150 m of their internal point. They keep the straight-line test, which can only count them nearer than they are, so for them the walking share is an upper bound.
Judged on one date, the build date of the transit data. A feed can run out of dates while buses still run, so a low value is not proof that service stopped.
Every resident of a block is placed at the block's internal point. Residents are 2020 Census counts, and the stops are those of the current transit data.
municipalities.pop_walk_active_pct.source_detail: 2020 Census block population and internal points (TIGERweb Census2020 layer 10); ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) and municipal GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) stops; roads from OpenStreetMap (site/data/roads.bin, ODbL)

municipalities.pop_served_method.plain: Residents are placed by 2020 Census block, and a block counts as served when a scheduled stop lies within 400 m. This entry gives the steps and the known limits.
municipalities.pop_served_method.plain_es: Las personas residentes se ubican por bloque censal del Censo de 2020, y un bloque cuenta como servido cuando hay una parada con horario a 400 m o menos. Esta entrada da los pasos y los límites conocidos.
municipalities.pop_served_method.definition: The observatory takes the 36,570 Census blocks of Puerto Rico that had at least one resident in 2020 (3,285,874 people). Each block's population sits at the block's internal point, the point inside the block that the Census Bureau stores (fields INTPTLAT and INTPTLON). The block's municipality is read from the county code in its ID, so each municipality's total equals population_2020 in all 78 municipalities. For each block: served is true when the nearest scheduled stop, from any feed, any municipality, is less than 401 m away (the distance is rounded down to whole metres); active is true when a stop of an operator whose feed has not expired is 400 m or less away; ATI is true when a stop of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) feed is 400 m or less away; municipal is true when a stop of any other feed is 400 m or less away. Each field adds the populations of the blocks with the flag.
municipalities.pop_served_method.method: network.coverage() runs in build.py and again in refresh_network.py. The overall served flag looks up the single nearest stop by latitude and longitude and rounds its distance in metres down to a whole number. The active, ATI and municipal flags look at every stop in a small search window around the block and then test the exact distance against 400 m, so the two tests can differ slightly.
municipalities.pop_served_method.how_to_read: The counts are estimates of how many people live near a stop. They treat everyone in a block as living at one point, so a large rural block with people spread along a road is approximated.
caveats: ATI plus municipal can exceed the overall count because people near both are counted in both. In the transit data built 2026-10-02, San Juan has 255,093 + 133,352 against 276,909 served.

The overall test and the other three tests differ slightly. In the transit data built 2026-10-02, recounting with exact distances gives 925,020 residents served island-wide instead of 925,788. 14 blocks (1,219 residents) count in the overall test only because their distance rounds down to 400 m. 4 blocks (451 residents) are missed because the nearest stop by coordinates is not the nearest in metres. The difference is under 1 percentage point in every municipality; the largest is Vega Baja (287 residents, 0.5 points).

In the transit data built 2026-10-02, pop_served_active_pct is higher than pop_served_pct in Carolina (58.1 against 57.9) and Manatí (30.4 against 30.3) for the same reason: it uses the exact distance.
Expired feeds count in the overall, ATI and municipal figures.
municipalities.pop_served_method.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb Census2020 layer 10); ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) and municipal GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) stops

municipalities.stop_kinds.plain: The observatory sorts every stop, station, terminal, airport, taxi stand and charger into one of eight kinds. This entry says how a scheduled stop differs from a mapped one and which kinds each municipal count adds up.
municipalities.stop_kinds.plain_es: El observatorio clasifica cada parada, estación, terminal, aeropuerto, parada de taxis y cargador en uno de ocho tipos. Esta entrada explica en qué se diferencia una parada con horario de una registrada en el mapa y qué tipos suma cada conteo municipal.
municipalities.stop_kinds.definition: A scheduled stop is any boarding point from a timetable feed (GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification) of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) or of a municipal system; it can have the kind transit stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal. A mapped stop is a point that volunteers added to OpenStreetMap; the observatory keeps it only when it does not duplicate a scheduled stop. A station or terminal is a larger facility: scheduled stops become stations by name or by the mode of the routes that serve them, and OpenStreetMap stations come from tags. The municipal fields count the kinds as follows: transit_stops adds transit stop, bus stop, bus station, rail station and ferry terminal; gtfs_stops adds every kind whose source is a timetable feed; bus_stations, rail_stations, ferry_terminals, airports, taxi_stands and ev_charging count one kind each.
municipalities.stop_kinds.method: The rules that give each point its kind are in transit.stop_kind.
municipalities.stop_kinds.how_to_read: Read a count by its kind. A high transit_stops value mixes scheduled stops and volunteer-mapped stops; gtfs_stops isolates the stops that have a timetable; stops_current, stops_expired and stops_osm split transit_stops by the state of the timetable. In the 2026-10 snapshot, transit_stops is 4,360 (transit stop 3,781, bus stop 459, bus station 91, rail station 16, ferry terminal 13) and gtfs_stops is 3,847 (transit stop 3,781, 44 scheduled bus stations, 16 rail stations, 6 scheduled ferry terminals). For the other kinds see the Codes table of transit.stop_kind.
caveats: The code can also read helipads and bike-rental points from OpenStreetMap; none appear in the 2026-10 snapshot (see transit.stop_kind).
A scheduled stop becomes a bus station by its name only.
municipalities.stop_kinds.source_detail: GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) feeds (ATI, municipal), kinds set in network.py parse_gtfs; OpenStreetMap tags, kinds set in transport.py osm_kind; FAA airports via BTS (Bureau of Transportation Statistics) NTAD (National Transportation Atlas Database)

municipalities.feed_status.plain: Each transit operator's public timetable is marked current, expiring, expired or none (no public feed found). The first three come from the timetable's end date. This entry defines the words current and active used in the transit fields.
municipalities.feed_status.plain_es: El horario público de cada operador de transporte colectivo se marca como vigente, por vencer, vencido o ninguno (no se encontró una fuente pública). Los tres primeros salen de la fecha de fin del horario. Esta entrada define las palabras vigente y activo que se usan en los campos de transporte colectivo.
municipalities.feed_status.definition: The state of an operator's timetable feed on the build date of the transit data (2026-10-02 in the current data). Current: the feed's end date is more than 60 days after the build date. Expiring: it ends within 60 days. Expired: the end date is earlier than the build date. None: the operator reports to the National Transit Database (NTD) but no public feed was found. In the pop_served_active_pct field, active means not expired, so current, expiring and unknown-date feeds are all active. The access fields of tourism places use a similar test: a stop has a current timetable when its operator's feed end date is on or after the date of the computation (access_as_of), so the current and expiring states both count and a feed with no end date does not. The end date is the latest end date among the feed's service calendars, or the feed's own end date when it has no calendar. The code also defines unknown (no end date) and broken (the feed could not be read).
municipalities.feed_status.method: network.py computes the state for every operator each time it builds or refreshes the network. The Transit tab recomputes current, expiring and expired from the end date when the page opens, using Puerto Rico's date, so a page opened later can show a newer state than the file.
municipalities.feed_status.how_to_read: A current feed has an end date more than 60 days away. The start date and holiday or other exceptions are not checked, and the end date is the latest of all the feed's calendars, so current does not show that every route runs on a valid timetable. It does not show that vehicles run on that timetable either. Expired means the dates ran out, which can happen while buses still run. In the transit data built 2026-10-02 there are 44 operators: 17 current (including the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, ATI), 1 expiring, 7 expired (all municipal), 16 none, 2 inside the ATI feed and 1 community. Unknown and broken do not occur. In the access fields, 'current timetable' covers the first two states: 18 feeds (17 current and 1 expiring, Canóvanas) against 7 expired.
caveats: Stops of expired feeds are still counted in gtfs_stops, transit_stops, stops_expired, transit_pct and pop_served_pct. They are left out of stops_current, the acc_ fields and pop_served_active_pct.
The observatory has no real-time vehicle data.

values.current: Timetable end date more than 60 days after the build date.
values.expiring: Timetable ends within 60 days of the build date.
values.expired: Timetable end date is before the build date.
values.none: On the NTD list but no public feed found.
values.in_ati: The buses of the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA) and the ferries of the Maritime Transport Authority, whose stops and routes are inside the feed of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI).
values.community: Routes mapped by volunteers in OpenStreetMap, with no timetable (públicos and other routes).

municipalities.feed_status.geography: Puerto Rico (all operators in the transit data)
municipalities.feed_status.source_detail: End dates in the ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) and municipal GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) feeds; operator list from the FTA (Federal Transit Administration) NTD

view.label: Map, Transit tab: operators and the state of their data

municipalities.walk_rule_400m.plain: The observatory treats a place or a block as near transit when a stop lies within 400 m (a quarter mile) in a straight line. This entry says which stops each measure uses.
municipalities.walk_rule_400m.plain_es: El observatorio considera que un lugar o un bloque está cerca del transporte colectivo cuando hay una parada a 400 m o menos (un cuarto de milla) en línea recta. Esta entrada indica qué paradas usa cada medida.
municipalities.walk_rule_400m.definition: The observatory counts a place or a block as near transit when a stop lies 400 m or less away in a straight line. The distance is a planning assumption, not a measure of how far people walk. All fixed distances are listed in transit.distance_rules. The distance is measured to a stop in any municipality. The measures use the rule with different stop sets. The walking measures for tourism places (tw_m in place_access.json; acc_walk400_pct, acc_walk800_pct and acc_wfreq400_pct; the barrio counts acc_walk400 and acc_wfreq400) apply the same 400 m and 800 m to the distance walked along mapped roads instead of the straight line (see place_access.tw_m). Tourism places near any mapped stop (places_near_transit, transit_pct): the nearest stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal of transit_stops, scheduled or volunteer-mapped, from any feed including those that have ended. Tourism places near a stop with a current timetable (acc_cur400_pct, acc_freq400_pct, acc_sat400_pct and acc_sun400_pct; acc_cur800_pct uses 800 m): scheduled stops of operators whose feed has not ended on access_as_of, with the distance rounded up to whole metres. Residents (pop_served_400m, pop_served_pct, pop_served_active_pct, pop_served_ati, pop_served_muni): scheduled stops only, measured from each Census block's internal point; pop_served_active_pct skips expired feeds. The overall resident share rounds the distance down to whole metres before it tests 400 m (see municipalities.pop_served_method).
municipalities.walk_rule_400m.method: Distance in metres = square root of (dlat × 111,320)² plus (dlng × 111,320 × cos(mean latitude))², with dlat and dlng in degrees. A place is near when its nearest stop is 400 m or less away; for the nearest stop with a current timetable the distance is rounded up to whole metres (ts_m), so ts_m of 400 or less is the test. Against a computation in projected metres the formula is about 0.6% long north to south, so a share can read up to 0.1 point lower. For the overall resident share, a block is near when the distance to its nearest stop, rounded down to whole metres, is 400 or less. For the resident figures that count the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) feed, the municipal feeds or active feeds, a block is near when any stop of that group is 400 m or less away.
municipalities.walk_rule_400m.how_to_read: Near means a short straight-line distance to a stop. It does not account for service frequency or hours, hills, rivers, fences, missing sidewalks or street crossings. A place 300 m from a stop across a highway counts as near.
caveats: The place measure acc_cur400_pct and the resident measure pop_served_active_pct both need a timetable that has not ended, so they can be compared. transit_pct also counts volunteer-mapped stops and stops of ended timetables, so it cannot be compared with the resident measures.
A distance is only as good as its points: a resident is placed at the block's internal point and a place at its listed coordinates.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: 400 m walk radius

municipalities.transit_data_updates.plain: Most transit fields now follow the nightly refresh. A few change only when the whole snapshot is rebuilt. This entry says which.
municipalities.transit_data_updates.plain_es: La mayoría de los campos de transporte colectivo ahora siguen la actualización de cada noche. Algunos cambian solo cuando se reconstruye todo el corte de datos. Esta entrada indica cuáles.
municipalities.transit_data_updates.definition: A full build (build.py) computes every transit field. A nightly job (refresh_network.py, which runs at 04:17 Puerto Rico time) re-reads the transit feeds. When a feed has changed, it rewrites in municipalities.json the fields pop_served_400m, pop_served_pct, pop_served_active_pct, pop_served_ati, pop_served_muni, muni_system and muni_system_routes, and the scheduled stops in transport.json. Every night, whether or not a feed changed, it then runs access.py, which recomputes from the stops file and rewrites only what changed: in municipalities.json the stop counts (transit_stops, gtfs_stops, bus_stations, rail_stations, ferry_terminals, airports, public_airports, taxi_stands, ev_charging, stops_current, stops_expired and stops_osm), places_near_transit, transit_pct, access_n, access_as_of and the acc_ fields; place_access.json; the transit_m, transit_400m and nearest_stop fields of places.json; and the access block and the count transport.places_near_transit in meta.json. It does not rebuild barrios.geojson (the barrio counts), the OpenStreetMap stops, the airports of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the Uber listing or the other fields of places.json. Those change at the next full build.
municipalities.transit_data_updates.method: Fields rewritten at night are recomputed from the feeds read that night (refresh_network.py) and, through access.py, from the stops file. All other transit fields are computed only at a full build. The Transit tab recalculates feed states from their end dates in the browser, against the date when the page is opened.
municipalities.transit_data_updates.how_to_read: Cite a transit field with the date of its data: the build date of the transit data (2026-10-02 in this snapshot) and, for the access fields, access_as_of (2026-10-06), not only the snapshot label, because the nightly refresh can change them without a new snapshot. The barrio counts are the exception: they keep the values of the last full build, so between full builds they can lag the municipality fields.
caveats: What the 2026-10 access update changed. The transit fields of places.json (transit_m, transit_400m and nearest_stop) and the stop counts of municipalities.json had gone out of date, so they were recomputed from today's stop list. 1,204 of the 35,118 places changed: the distance by more than 2 m for 892 and by 1 or 2 m for 152 (all shorter), and the stop name only for 160. 130 places gained the 400 m flag and none lost it; 129 of them are in Jayuya, whose 58 stops had a longitude without its minus sign when the places were last measured (all 183 places in Jayuya changed). Stop counts changed in six municipalities: Jayuya 0 to 54, Culebra 59 to 1, Utuado 47 to 50, Caguas 304 to 305, Juncos 129 to 128 and San Lorenzo 158 to 159. The share of places near any mapped stop changed in Jayuya (0.0 to 70.7) and Ponce (79.0 to 79.1). On the default basis the island count went from 12,369 places (46.5%) to 12,481 (47.0%). The residents-served fields did not change.
The access fields keep the date of the last run that changed a value (access_as_of). A run that finds no change writes nothing, so an older date does not mean that the refresh did not run.

measures.wait_between_departures.plain: How many minutes, on average, pass between one departure and the next in a part of the day: the morning peak (06:00-09:00), midday (09:00-15:00), the afternoon peak (15:00-19:00) and the evening (19:00-23:00).
measures.wait_between_departures.definition: The length of the period in minutes divided by the trips of a stop pattern that leave in it. Blank when no trip leaves in the period. For a route, the morning peak wait is that of its busiest pattern (one direction).
measures.wait_between_departures.method: supply.py: periods[name].hw = (minutes in the period) / (trips in the period), rounded.
measures.wait_between_departures.how_to_read: Planners often treat 15 minutes or less as service people can use without a timetable. An average hides irregular timetables: a route with 4 trips in 3 hours averages 45 minutes even if two of them leave together.
caveats: An average over the period, not the longest wait; see Longest wait at a stop.
measures.wait_between_departures.geography: Each stop pattern and route with a timetable

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: Existing routes
Route planner: Existing service near this route

measures.planner_existing_service.plain: For a route drawn in the route planner: the stops with a current timetable within 400 m of it, their departures between 7:00 and 8:00 on a weekday, the share of the route with no such stop within 400 m, and the routes that stop near it.
measures.planner_existing_service.definition: Stops with a current timetable (transit_supply.json, weekday) within 400 m in a straight line of the planned route; departures from them in the 07:00 hour; the share of points every 100 to 500 m along the route (depending on its length) with no such stop within 400 m; and the routes departing from those stops with their weekday trips and morning-peak wait. The residents count beside it (residents with no stop with a current timetable within 400 m) uses the same current stops.
measures.planner_existing_service.method: plan.js (score), on a grid of about 500 m of the current stops.
measures.planner_existing_service.how_to_read: A planned route that runs along existing frequent service adds little; one with a high share far from any current stop, and many residents near it, points to a gap. A planning aid, not a demand forecast.
caveats: Straight-line distances.
Públicos are in no timetable.
Before this measure, the residents count treated stops with an expired timetable as service; it now counts only current timetables when the supply file loads.
measures.planner_existing_service.geography: A route drawn by the user

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: plan a route
Map, Transit tab: plan a route

measures.frequent_service.plain: A stop has frequent service in an hour when 4 or more departures leave from it in that hour, any route.
measures.frequent_service.definition: frequent_per_hour in transit_supply.json (4). The island counts (island.frequent_stops) give, for each hour, the stops with a current timetable that reach it.
measures.frequent_service.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, about 280 stops have frequent service in each weekday hour from 07:00 to 18:00 (282 at 08:00), out of 2,261 stops with a departure in that hour. The access measures use another threshold (20 or more weekday departures in the day); say which one a figure uses.

view.label: 3D view, Time tab: Service at this hour

measures.longest_wait_at_stop.plain: The longest time between two departures at a stop between 06:00 and 22:00, counting from 06:00 to the first departure and from the last departure to 22:00.
measures.longest_wait_at_stop.definition: The largest gap, in minutes, between consecutive departures at the stop (any route), with 06:00 and 22:00 as the edges of the window. Blank when the stop has no departure in the window.
measures.longest_wait_at_stop.how_to_read: A stop with many departures can still have a long gap in the middle of the day. In the 2026-10 snapshot, even the busiest weekday stops (254 departures) have a longest wait of 18 to 28 minutes.

view.label: 3D view: click a stop of Stops by departures in the hour

layers.route_profile_3d.plain: Choose an existing route to see its service hour by hour, the wait between departures in each direction, its stops and the routes of any operator that stop within 250 m of it. The route is highlighted on the map, with its stops and the stops of the connecting routes.
layers.route_profile_3d.definition: The Existing routes section of the Route tab. The card shows the route's operator and mode, whether its timetable is current (with the feed's end date), trips on a weekday, Saturday and Sunday, first and last departure, the morning-peak wait of its busiest direction, departures by hour, a table of its directions (stop patterns) with trips, the average wait in four periods, run time, length and scheduled speed, the stops of its busiest direction with each stop's departures (all routes) and longest wait, and its connections: routes with a weekday departure from a stop within 250 m of one of its stops, other operators first.
layers.route_profile_3d.method: supply3d.js, from transit_supply.json, the trips files (paths and path_stops), transport.json (stop names and positions) and operators.json (feed dates). Connections are found on a grid of the stops with weekday departures, by straight-line distance.
layers.route_profile_3d.how_to_read: Connections are places where two routes can meet, by distance only: the card does not yet check whether their times fit (a short wait to change). Phase 3 of the transit analysis plan adds that.
caveats: 250 m in a straight line, not a walking route.
Timetables, not observed service.

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: Existing routes

layers.service_at_this_hour_3d.plain: Routes drawn by the trips they run in the hour on the clock, and stops sized by their departures in that hour, for a weekday, Saturday or Sunday, with a chart of vehicles in service through the day.
layers.service_at_this_hour_3d.definition: Two switches and a summary in the Time tab of the 3D view. Routes by trips in the hour draws each stop pattern with trips in that hour along its path, by trips per hour (1, 2-3, 4-5, 6 or more). Stops by departures in the hour draws each stop with a departure in that hour, by its departures. The summary gives, for the hour, vehicles in service, routes running, stops with a departure and stops with frequent service; the chart gives vehicles in service for every hour (click a bar to move the clock). A click on a route or a stop of these layers opens its card, before the map's own features drawn under it: a stop of the Stops layer, a cluster of stops, a route line or an area. The day buttons (Weekday, Saturday, Sunday) choose the timetable for the replay and for these layers. Expired timetables are left out unless Include operators whose timetable has expired is checked.
layers.service_at_this_hour_3d.method: supply3d.js reads transit_supply.json and the paths of the day's trips file; the layers change when the hour on the clock changes.
layers.service_at_this_hour_3d.how_to_read: Play the day to see where service starts, peaks and stops. Places with no line or dot in an hour have no scheduled service then. Click a route for its trips in the hour and a link to its profile; click a stop for its departures, routes and longest wait.
caveats: Where several routes share a road, the lines overlap; the widest shows the busiest route, not their total.
Públicos are in no timetable.

view.label: 3D view, Time tab: Service at this hour

measures.span_of_service.plain: The time of the first and the last departure of the day for a route, a direction or a stop.
measures.span_of_service.definition: The earliest and the latest departure from the first stop (for a pattern or route) or from the stop (for a stop), in seconds after midnight in the file and as hours and minutes on the page.
measures.span_of_service.method: supply.py: first and last of the sorted departure times.
measures.span_of_service.how_to_read: A short span leaves out early workers and evening trips home even when the peak service is good.
measures.span_of_service.geography: Each stop pattern, route and stop with a timetable

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: Existing routes

transit.stop_pattern.plain: The trips of a route that stop at the same places in the same order. A route usually has at least two, one for each direction, and more when some trips skip stops or end early.
transit.stop_pattern.definition: A stop pattern is the ordered list of stops of a trip. Trips with the same operator, route label and stops, in the same order, share one pattern. trip_paths.py stores each pattern once, as a path along the route line (paths), with its stop ids (path_stops); each trip names its pattern (k). In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 3,297 weekday trips share 222 patterns.
transit.stop_pattern.method: trip_paths.py groups the trips of each day by operator, route label and the coordinates of their stops, in order.
transit.stop_pattern.how_to_read: Supply by pattern is supply in one direction. A route's total adds up its patterns, so it counts both directions.

transit.supply_file.plain: How much scheduled service each route, each direction of a route and each stop has, hour by hour, on a weekday, a Saturday and a Sunday. It is built from the published timetables, so it shows the service operators plan, not the service that ran.
transit.supply_file.definition: transit_supply.json has one section per day type (wk: a typical weekday; sa: Saturday; su: Sunday). Each section has four parts. patterns: one row per stop pattern (see Stop pattern), with the operator (o), route (r), mode (m), whether the operator's timetable is current (cur), number of stops, length along the route line in km, trips, trips per hour (hours, 24 values by the hour of the departure from the first stop), first and last departure in seconds after midnight, trips and average wait in four periods (periods: am 06:00-09:00, mid 09:00-15:00, pm 15:00-19:00, eve 19:00-23:00), median run time in minutes, scheduled speed in km/h, and whether the path follows the route line (line). routes: one row per operator and route label, adding up its patterns (both directions), with peak_hw, the average wait at the morning peak of its busiest pattern. stops: one row per stop id (the ids of transport.json) with departures (n), departures per hour (hours), the routes that depart from it, first and last departure and the longest wait between 06:00 and 22:00 (gap, minutes). island: for each hour, vehicles in service, routes running, stops with a departure and stops with frequent service (frequent_per_hour, 4: a departure every 15 minutes or better), counting only current timetables. In the 2026-10 snapshot, a weekday has 222 stop patterns, 144 routes and 2,866 stops with departures; 38 of the 144 routes run on an expired timetable.
transit.supply_file.method: supply.py reads trips.json, trips_sa.json and trips_su.json (format 2: each trip's stop pattern, where its stops are on the pattern's path and its stop times; trip_paths.py) and the feed status of each operator in operators.json. A trip counts in the hour of its departure from its first stop. A departure is every stop time of a trip except its last stop, where the vehicle arrives. The average wait in a period is the period's length divided by its trips (180 minutes and 6 trips give 30 minutes); it is not the longest wait. Run time is the median of the pattern's trips; the scheduled speed is its length along the route line over that time. A row is current (cur) when its operator's feed status is current or expiring on the day of the build.
transit.supply_file.how_to_read: Use the patterns to compare service by direction, the routes to compare routes, and the stops to see where and when people can board. Look at trips per hour and the wait at the peak together with the span (first and last departure): a route with a short wait but service only in the morning serves fewer trips in a day than its peak suggests. Compare current and expired timetables separately.
caveats: Timetables, not observed service: a trip may not run, run late or be added without the feed saying so.
Expired timetables (cur false) may still run, run differently, or not run at all.
Públicos are in no timetable, so they are not counted; where públicos run, the real service is higher.
About 8.9% of weekday stop calls have no time in the feeds and are not counted as departures.
The average wait is a planning figure for the whole period. Irregular timetables can have much longer single waits; the longest wait at each stop (gap) shows that.

economy.no_vehicle_hh_pct.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many have no car, truck or van available. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 13.0% in 2020-2024, down from 20.3% in 2006-2010.
economy.no_vehicle_hh_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos no tienen carro, camioneta ni van disponible. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 13.0% en 2020-2024, menos que el 20.3% de 2006-2010.
economy.no_vehicle_hh_pct.definition: Households with no vehicle available, divided by all households (occupied housing units), times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B25044. The top adds cell 3 (owner-occupied homes with no vehicle) and cell 10 (renter-occupied homes with no vehicle). The bottom is cell 1, all occupied housing units.
economy.no_vehicle_hh_pct.method: The observatory reads table B25044 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 3 and 10 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.no_vehicle_hh_pct.how_to_read: A value of 13 means that 13 of every 100 households had no vehicle available. It is a count of households, not of people, and it says nothing about whether a household wants a vehicle or has transit nearby. For transit access, see the share of residents near a scheduled stop. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B25044 (Tenure by Vehicles Available), cells 3 and 10 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: It counts occupied homes only. Empty homes are not in the base.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.8 to ±8.1 points across the 78 municipalities, and 8 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate. In the same snapshot, San Juan has the highest value for 2020-2024, 20.78% (± 0.85 points), and Toa Alta the lowest, 5.5% (± 1.0 points).

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 11.9% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 13.0%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra goes from 17.18% (2017-2021) to 24.16% (2018-2022). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 93% of barrios and 96% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
economy.no_vehicle_hh_pct.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts
economy.no_vehicle_hh_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B25044 (Tenure by Vehicles Available), cells 001, 003 and 010; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

energy.page.plain: The figures of the Energy in Puerto Rico page: where electricity comes from since 2010, rooftop solar and batteries, use and smart meters by municipio, reliability, price and the grid's exposure to floods.
energy.page.plain_es: Las cifras de la página Energía en Puerto Rico: de dónde viene la electricidad desde 2010, la solar en techos y las baterías, el consumo y los contadores inteligentes por municipio, la confiabilidad, el precio y la exposición de la red a las inundaciones.
energy.page.definition: energy.json: series (months, gen_gwh by source: oil, gas, coal, hydro, solar, wind, landfill and dg, the energy rooftop systems export; rps_pct; rooftop_customers; rooftop_mw; exported_gwh), annual_gwh (full years), capacity (EIA-860M by technology and rooftop MW), municipios (ids, names, housing units, residents, batteries and their kWh, electricity sales in the last 12 months, smart-meter share, bess_series), districts (rooftop solar MW and installations by LUMA commercial district), saidi (monthly SAIDI of transmission and distribution, its distribution part, by technical district, and EIA-861's 2025 figures), price (Puerto Rico's and the United States' residential cents per kWh), exposure (line km and plant MW inside FEMA's 1% flood area and V zones), lines_km, lines_as_of and law (the renewable targets of Act 17-2019 and Act 1-2025).
energy.page.method: energy_series.py reads LUMA's Exhibit 2 of the distributed generation data (case NEPR-MI-2019-0016) and monthly metrics workbook (case NEPR-MI-2019-0007) from the Energy Bureau's site, EIA-861M's sales to ultimate customers, and the observatory's power_plants.geojson, power_lines.geojson, flood.geojson and municipios.geojson. San Juan's three LUMA areas (San Juan, Río Piedras, Santurce) are added together. Solar, wind and landfill gas production are read from Exhibit 2's contracted renewable production; its second set of columns for these fuels holds other quantities before October 2017.
energy.page.how_to_read: Open the Knowledge Area page Energy in Puerto Rico (energy.html). Production by source runs from 2010-01 to 2026-06; batteries, sales and SAIDI from 2021-06 to 2026-09; the residential price from 2021-01 to 2026-08.
caveats: Production includes only the energy rooftop systems send to the grid, not what homes use themselves.
LUMA's monthly SAIDI counts transmission and distribution outages; outages from a lack of generation are not in it. EIA-861's 2025 figure counts every event.
Electricity sales by municipio include homes, businesses, industry and government.
The 38 kV lines are about half mapped in OpenStreetMap, so their flood figures are a lower bound.
energy.page.geography: Puerto Rico; 78 municipios; LUMA's 34 commercial and 16 technical districts
energy.page.source_detail: LUMA Exhibit 2 (sheet Monthly) and metrics workbook (sheet T&D); EIA-861M sales_ult_cust (territory and state sheets); EIA-860M via power_plants.geojson

layers.powerlines.plain: OpenStreetMap's high-voltage lines on the map, coloured and sized by voltage (230, 115 and 38 kV) and drawn simplified to about 100 m; substations are counted, not drawn.
layers.powerlines.plain_es: Las líneas de alto voltaje de OpenStreetMap en el mapa, con color y grosor según el voltaje (230, 115 y 38 kV) y dibujadas simplificadas a unos 100 m; las subestaciones se cuentan, no se dibujan.
layers.powerlines.definition: power_lines.geojson: OpenStreetMap's ways tagged power=line or power=cable with a voltage of 230, 115 or 38 kV (the highest of the way's 'voltage' tag), joined by voltage and simplified to about 100 m; one MultiLineString per voltage and kind. Each has kv (230, 115 or 38), km (the length mapped at that voltage and kind, measured before simplifying) and cable (true for an underground or submarine cable). The notes give km by voltage, the km left out (281 km with no voltage tag), and the 549 substations mapped, by voltage class and by municipio. No name, operator, circuit number, tower or substation point is kept.
layers.powerlines.method: power_lines.py asks the Overpass API (no key) for power=line, power=cable and power=substation inside Puerto Rico's box. A way's voltage is the highest value of its 'voltage' tag; only 230, 115 and 38 kV are drawn. Ways of the same voltage and kind are joined (shapely linemerge) and simplified with Douglas-Peucker at 0.0009 degrees, about 100 m. Substations are placed in the municipio whose outline holds them (the centre of a mapped outline) and only counted (HANDOFF decision 104 (c)).
layers.powerlines.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Infrastructure and mobility: Energy), with Power plants. The 230 kV backbone (752 km) runs from the south-coast plants (Aguirre, Costa Sur, EcoEléctrica, AES) over the Cordillera Central to the north, where most electricity is used; the 115 kV (900 km) and 38 kV (1,052 km) networks spread from it to the towns. Click a line for its voltage and the length mapped at that voltage.
caveats: The 38 kV network is about half mapped: 1,052 km in OpenStreetMap against 2,214 km of 38 kV circuits in the utility's 2019 Integrated Resource Plan. A gap in it is a gap in the map, not on the ground.

The 115 kV network has about 82% of the length the 2019 plan lists (900 km against 1,130 km of circuits); the 230 kV network is complete. Circuit length counts each circuit, so two circuits on one tower line count twice in the plan and once here.

The lines are simplified to about 100 m: they show where the network runs, not each tower or the exact path. The utility asks the Energy Bureau to treat the location of its lines as Critical Energy Infrastructure Information, which is why the layer keeps no name, operator or circuit number and draws no substation.
Distribution lines (13.2 kV and below, along the streets) are not in this layer.
layers.powerlines.geography: Lines over Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra
layers.powerlines.source_detail: OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API: ways tagged power=line or power=cable (tag voltage), and ways and nodes tagged power=substation (counted only)

infrastructure.power_mw.definition: The nameplate capacity of the operating generators of the municipality, in megawatts. Batteries are left out: they store power.
infrastructure.power_mw.method: infrastructure_series.py reads the newest EIA-860M file (sheet Operating_PR) and places each operating generator in the municipality whose boundary holds the plant's point (the county field is blank for about a third of them). Each plant's point, name and capacity are also published as the Power plants map layer (power_plants.geojson); owner names are not kept.

caveats: Nameplate capacity is what generators are built to produce, not what they produce or can produce today.

layers.plants.plain: Every power plant of 1 MW or more on the map, as the US Energy Information Administration lists them each month: the area of each circle is the plant's capacity and its colour is the technology with the most capacity.
layers.plants.plain_es: Todas las plantas de energía de 1 MW o más en el mapa, como las lista cada mes la Administración de Información Energética de EE. UU.: el área de cada círculo es la capacidad de la planta y su color es la tecnología con más capacidad.
layers.plants.definition: power_plants.geojson: one point per plant in the Puerto Rico sheets of EIA-860M (67 plants with an operating generator in 40 municipios and 1 planned plant in the file of September 2026). Each point has name (as EIA writes it), type, municipio, geoid, eia (EIA's plant id), tech (the main technology: oil, gas, coal, solar, wind, hydro, battery or landfill), mw (operating nameplate MW without batteries), bat_mw and bat_mwh (batteries, in MW and MWh), by (MW by technology), sb (MW on standby), out (MW out of service), units (operating generators), y0 and y1 (the first and last year a generator entered service), plan and plan_ym (MW planned or under construction, and the earliest expected month) and status (op or planned). Four more points have status built: large solar plants that are built but not yet in commercial operation, so not yet in EIA-860M (energy_src/plants_added.json, November 2026: CIRO One Salinas 90 MW, the two Marahú farms in Salinas and Jobos, Guayama, 120 and 80 MW, and Yabucoa Solar 32.1 MW). They have no eia id; they have stage (connected: connected to the grid, commercial operation not yet declared; complete: construction complete, not yet connected), as_of (the month of that status), src and url (the source) and osm (the OpenStreetMap ways whose outlines place the point).
layers.plants.method: power_plants.py reads the newest EIA-860M workbook (no key), sheets Operating_PR and Planned_PR, and adds up each plant's generators by technology group. The point is EIA's, and it places the plant in the municipio whose outline holds it. The main technology is the one with the most operating nameplate MW without batteries (batteries when a plant has nothing else). The map draws each circle with an area in proportion to that MW: a radius of 0.55 times the square root of the MW, in pixels, and at least 3. A planned plant is drawn hollow. Owner names (EIA's Entity Name) are never kept (HANDOFF decision 104 (b)). The built plants come from a list kept by hand (energy_src/plants_added.json), each with its source: the Energy Bureau's filings for status and the press for capacity and batteries. Each point is the area-weighted centre of the plant's outlines in OpenStreetMap, which mappers traced from Esri World Imagery; Esri's Wayback imagery dates each build. For Marahú, AES gives 120 MW for its Salinas site and 80 MW for Jobos; the larger of the two new farms (164 ha, at the Salinas–Guayama line, most of it inside Guayama's census outline) is taken as the Salinas site. A built plant leaves the file by itself once EIA lists a plant whose name matches it. The totals in the notes (plants, MW, renewable MW, batteries) stay EIA's operating plants; built_plants, built_mw and built_battery_mw count the added ones.
layers.plants.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Infrastructure and mobility: Energy). The largest circles are the utility's oil and gas plants on the south and north coasts (Aguirre 1,534 MW in Salinas, Costa Sur 1,032 MW in Guayanilla, San Juan 840 MW). Click a plant for its capacity by technology, batteries, standby, years in service and EIA's plant number. Puerto Rico had 67 plants with 6,436.1 MW in September 2026, 397.7 MW of it renewable, and 38.2 MW of batteries.
caveats: Nameplate capacity is what the generators are built to produce, not what they produce or can produce today. EIA counts generators on standby and out of service with the operating ones; the pop-up says how much.

Rooftop solar is not in this inventory: each system is under 1 MW. LUMA's monthly metrics, filed with the Puerto Rico Energy Bureau, counted 1,666 MW of rooftop solar at 209,404 installations in September 2026, more than four times the renewable capacity of these plants.
Factories, hospitals and federal sites appear with their own generators, many of which run only when the grid fails.
The colour is one technology per plant; a plant can have more (Costa Sur has natural gas and oil units). The pop-up lists them all.

The four built solar plants (322.1 MW, and 336.5 MW of batteries) are drawn dashed and are not in the totals: in November 2026 CIRO One was connected to the grid but had no commercial operation date, the two Marahú farms were built but not connected, and Yabucoa Solar was complete with its first synchronization scheduled. Utility-scale solar that is contracted but not built (the rest of the procurement tranches 1, 2 and 4, such as Guayama Solar, Xzerta-Tec Solar I, the Go Green parks in Yabucoa and Naguabo, San Juan Solar and Marisol Power) is not drawn: the filings checked give no site.

infrastructure.power_renewable_mw.definition: The nameplate capacity of the operating solar, wind, hydroelectric and landfill gas generators of the municipality, in megawatts.
infrastructure.power_renewable_mw.method: infrastructure_series.py reads the newest EIA-860M file (sheet Operating_PR) and places each operating generator in the municipality whose boundary holds the plant's point (the county field is blank for about a third of them). Each plant's point, name and capacity are also published as the Power plants map layer (power_plants.geojson); owner names are not kept.
infrastructure.power_renewable_mw.how_to_read: 397.7 MW for Puerto Rico; the largest in Santa Isabel 101.2 MW, Isabela 45.0 MW, Yauco 34.0 MW.
caveats: Rooftop solar, which is large in Puerto Rico, is not in EIA's inventory.
infrastructure.power_renewable_mw.source_detail: EIA-860M monthly generator file, sheet Operating_PR: Plant ID, Technology, Nameplate Capacity (MW), Status, Latitude, Longitude
